title: Controlling Conditional Language Models without Catastrophic Forgetting

gain_metric: average number of PEP8 violations per generated function (pycodestyle)
baseline_name: DPG-like ablation (closest contender) and the original pretrained GPT-Neo a
gain_note: No numeric PEP8 result exists anywhere in the text: the PEP8 error count is reported only as a curve in Fig. 4b (and violation-type bar charts in Fig. 5b), both of which the PDF extraction renders as stray axis numbers. The running text gives only the pre-fine-tuning level ('a Python function generated by GPT-Neo will compile only 40% of the time and will contain on average 4 violations of PEP8') and a qualitative claim that CDPG 'decrease[s] the average number of PEP8 violations'. The one quotable pair of numbers in the code-generation section, 'increase the fraction of compilable functions from around 40% to around 65%', is syntactic correctness, not the R/M outcome, so it is not used as the gain.
core_idea: Express a control objective (zero pycodestyle violations) as a conditional energy-based model that multiplies the pretrained model's distribution by a binary constraint scorer, then fine-tune the model with conditional distributional policy gradients to approximate it, satisfying the constraint while staying close to the original distribution.
core_idea_checked: Section 2: a conditional EBM Pc(x) = a(x|c) b(x,c) is defined per context; CDPG minimises the expected cross-entropy between the model and the normalised pc by importance sampling from the model itself, estimating the per-context partition function Zc from a batch of M samples (Algorithm 1). For the code objective, c is a Python function signature from Python150 and b(x,c)=1 iff pycodestyle reports zero violations.
note: The method itself is domain-agnostic and operates on ordinary Python function generation, but the paper never evaluates functional correctness of the generated code and reports the PEP8 outcome only in plots.

title: From Experience to Expertise: Adoption-Aware Memory Learning for Data-Scarce NPU Kernel Synthesis
technique_name: SAGE (Adoption-Traced Utility estimation + Utility-Gated Consolidation) persistent memory-learning kernel-synthesis agent
metrics: efficiency: Fast1.0 = fraction of solved operators whose best kernel beats the torch_npu reference latency (execution); Sself = median Tfirst/Tbest within-episode speedup (execution); per-operator speedup over torch_npu, latency measured with torch.npu.Event device-side timers, 5 warm-up + 100 timed iterations, mean per-execution latency (execution). correctness (co-outcome): Execution Rate and Compilation Rate on NPUKernelBench, correctness defined by max_abs_error <= 1e-3 and max_rel_error <= 1e-3 versus torch_npu (execution). Mechanism check: expert rating of adoption records (human).
benchmarks: NPUKernelBench, coverage-oriented 88-operator subset (20 Level-1, 50 Level-2, all 18 Level-3); transfer set of 16 xCCL operators; task-order study on 25 Level-2 source operators and 18 Level-3 targets
models: Qwen3-Coder-Next, 80B, open, code-specialized instruct; DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 284B, open, instruct; GLM-5.2, 744B, open, instruct; GLM-5.3 (used on the xCCL transfer set); all frozen backbones served locally via vllm-ascend
baselines: Refinement (iterative repair/optimization, no cross-task memory); Static RAG (same initial cold memory and retrieval pipeline, memory writes and utility updates disabled); Value Memory (EvoKernel-style value-driven cross-task memory with uniform credit assignment); ablations: Uniform Credit, w/o UGC, Random UGC; frozen-bank controls: Relevance Only, Uniform Credit, ATU
effect_target_headline: With GLM-5.2, "Relative to Value Memory, Fast1.0 increases from 75.7% to 86.9%, while median Sself improves from 3.36× to 4.47×" on the 88-operator NPUKernelBench subset; "With GLM-5.3, SAGE achieves a 43.99× speedup over the torch_npu reference on sparse flash attention"
effect_correctness_headline: "On NPUKernelBench, SAGE achieves a 95.5% execution rate versus 84.1% for the strongest controlled baseline, with 86.9% of solved operators outperforming torch_npu" (GLM-5.2, 88-operator subset); Level-3 ER 88.9% vs 61.1% for Value Memory
notes: Table 1 (main results) is garbled by PDF extraction: rows and columns are interleaved, so per-cell values other than the ones quoted in the running text should be re-checked against the PDF. Figures 3-5 are reported as extracted label text only. No artifact/code URL is given (only the third-party OpenCode repository). No repeated runs, variance or statistical tests; single run per configuration, medians used because of the long-tailed speedup distribution (0.38x to 71.41x). Contamination is addressed only indirectly: cold-start differential-mining operators are stated to be disjoint from the 88 evaluation operators, and anti-hacking safeguards forbid expert-implementation leakage and semantic shortcuts, but pretraining contamination of the backbones is not discussed. Limitations appear in the conclusion rather than a dedicated threats-to-validity section. Compute reporting is limited to the 30-round interaction budget and a 10K-token resident memory budget; no token counts, wall-clock agent time, or dollar cost.
family_reason: The contribution is an external experience memory with hybrid sparse-dense retrieval, utility-based reranking and consolidation of rules into a resident context; the refinement loop and compiler/profiler feedback are already present in the Refinement baseline, so the retrieval/memory machinery is what adds the gain.
scope_reason: The outcome is the runtime efficiency (measured latency versus the torch_npu reference) of kernels the LLM agent generates, alongside execution correctness.
gain_metric: Fast1.0 (fraction of solved operators whose best kernel beats the torch_npu reference latency), GLM-5.2 on the 88-operator NPUKernelBench subset
baseline_name: Value Memory (EvoKernel-style value-driven cross-task memory, the strongest controlled baseline)
gain_quote: Relative to Value Memory, Fast1.0 increases from 75.7% to 86.9%,
gain_note: Section 4.2, running text for Table 1 (Table 1 itself is garbled by PDF extraction into interleaved column blocks, so only the running-text numbers are reliable). The same sentence continues 'while median Sself improves from 3.36x to 4.47x'. Secondary efficiency claim: with GLM-5.3 on the xCCL transfer set, sparse flash attention speedup over torch_npu rises from 23.35x to 43.99x. All baselines are controlled re-implementations under the same OpenCode harness; no system-level comparison with published state of the art is made.
core_idea: Keep the backbone frozen and evolve an external memory of kernel-writing experiences, assigning credit only to experiences the agent recorded as actually adopted (Adoption-Traced Utility) and promoting repeatedly adopted, cross-operator-validated experiences into a bounded always-resident rule context (Utility-Gated Consolidation).
core_idea_checked: Sections 3.3-3.4: ATU records a per-item adoption state via a trace-completeness hook that blocks evaluation until every retrieved item is resolved, converts the terminal episode score (correctness pass, or relative latency reduction Tbest/Tfirst) into item-level credit shared among adopted items with a fixed penalty for unused retrievals, and updates a bandit-style utility used to rerank retrieval; UGC admits items with positive utility, at least Kado=3 adoptions and Kop=3 distinct adopting operators, abstracts them into resident rules, and greedily fills a 10K-token hot memory by utility per token with usage decay and demotion.
note: Tied to Ascend NPU kernel synthesis: the memory, cold-start knowledge, diagnostics (msDebug, msProf, AscendC probes) and the whole evaluation (NPUKernelBench, xCCL operators, Ascend 910C hardware) are accelerator-kernel specific, so it cannot run on general-purpose function-level benchmarks.

title: The FM Agent

metrics: efficiency: speedup of the generated CUDA kernel relative to torch.compile, measured by execution with 32 warmup and 128 profiling iterations (execution); kernel-level speedup against the official PyTorch implementation in the CosyVoice2-0.5B case study (execution). correctness (co-outcome): numerical tolerance tightened from 1e-2 to 1e-4 for acceptance, with reported accuracy maintained within 1e-5 (execution). models: Gemini-2.5-Pro, size undisclosed, closed, instruct/reasoning (used for FM Agent and for the OpenEvolve baseline in the controlled kernel comparison)
baselines: torch.compile (reference for kernel speedup); OpenEvolve powered by the same Gemini-2.5-Pro; AI CUDA Engineer (agentic SOTA); CUDA-L1 (RL SOTA); for the ablation: random sampling, top-k sampling, no cold start, no island model, and OpenEvolve

effect_correctness_headline: "maintaining numerical accuracy within 10−5"; acceptance tolerance tightened from 10−2 to 10−4; no per-task correctness or compilation rate is reported for KernelBench

Figures 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 are extracted as label fragments only. Variance is reported for MLE-Bench (3 runs, SEM) and the ahc016 ablation (5 runs, standard deviation) but not for the kernel results. An optional human-in-the-loop module is described, but the authors state that for all three benchmarks optimization was performed exclusively by the LLM without human intervention. No threats-to-validity section and no contamination discussion.
family_reason: An island-model evolutionary search repeatedly mutates candidate programs and keeps those that the execution-based evaluators score best, so evaluator feedback drives the gains.
scope_reason: The kernel experiment measures the runtime speedup of LLM-generated CUDA kernels; the other benchmarks (MLE-Bench, ALE-Bench, math) are task scores, not code quality.
gain_metric: speedup of generated CUDA kernel over torch.compile (KernelBench Level 3 subset, A100)
gain_quote: Our approach achieves 2.08× to 20.77× speedups over torch.compile

core_idea: A multi-agent cold-start generates a diverse initial population, then an island-model evolutionary search with adaptive diversity-driven sampling, guided by domain-specific evaluators (correctness, performance, LLM judge), iteratively improves programs on a distributed Ray cluster.
core_idea_checked: Two stages: a cold-start stage where several generation agents (optionally expert-guided) build a diverse initial pool, and an evolve stage where clustered islands evolve programs through mutation and crossover with cluster-based adaptive sampling and an elite pool, scored by fitness and LLM-judge evaluators, run asynchronously on Ray.
note: The framework itself is domain-agnostic (also applied to ML, combinatorial optimization and math), but its only non-functional evidence is a small, undocumented KernelBench Level 3 subset reported as a speedup range.

title: Translating Large-Scale C Repositories to Idiomatic Rust
technique_name: Rustine (preprocessing + automated C refactoring for unary operators, pointer arithmetic, constness maximization and large-function breakdown; dependence-graph-guided context and translation order; RAG-based API translation; two-tier LLM translation loop with compiler feedback and adaptive in-context-learning examples; test-based validation and delta-debugging-inspired repair)
metrics: security / memory safety: number of raw pointer declarations and dereferences, number of pointer arithmetic / comparison operations, number of unsafe lines, type casts and calls (all tool-static, via pycparser for C and the rustc_hir crate for Rust). readability-maintainability: idiomaticity = TSI x Clippy flags per KLoC where TSI = LoC_Rust / LoC_C and flags cover cargo, complexity, correctness, perf and suspicious lints (tool-static, Clippy); Cognitive Complexity, Halstead and SEI Maintainability Index (tool-static, rust-code-analysis); number of clippy::style violations (tool-static). correctness (co-outcome): percentage application- and test-code compilation success, and assertion pass rate from executing the translated test suites (execution). Also reported: translation time, dollar cost and token counts; human repair effort in hours.
benchmarks: 23 real-world C repositories taken from the artifacts of prior C-to-Rust work, 27 to 13,200 LoC (qsort, bst, rgba, quadtree, buffer, grabc, urlparser, xzoom, genann, ht, robotfindskitten, libcsv, avl-tree, libopenaptx, libtree, opl, libzahl, zopfli, snudown, lodepng, bzip2, binn, tulipindicator); test suites manually augmented to 1,221,192 assertions with average function and line coverage of 74.7% and 72.2%
models: DeepSeek-V3, size not stated, open-weight, instruct (base translator); DeepSeek-R1, size not stated, open-weight, reasoning (fallback after 8 failed attempts); OpenAI o4-mini, closed, reasoning (used only to synthesize adaptive in-context-learning examples)
baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpiler), C2SaferRust, CROWN, Laertes, RustMamp, Syzygy; plus an internal ablation of Rustine with the pointer-arithmetic refactoring component removed
effect_target_headline: "the number of raw pointer declarations/derefenreces is reduced from 4,080/2,045 in C to 198/126 in Rust"; pointer arithmetic reduced by refactoring "from 452 to 14"; ablation without pointer-arithmetic refactoring: "the number of pointer arithmetic increases by 83.01%, raw pointer declarations/dereferences by 52.6%/154%, and unsafe ⟨lines,type casts,calls⟩ by ⟨64.42%, 31.67%, 61.46%⟩"; versus baselines, "C2Rust, C2SaferRust, CROWN, and Laertes have 4,904/20,169, 1,400/5,510, 3,027/12,298, and 2,255/9,685 more raw pointer declarations and dereferences"; unsafe ⟨lines,type casts,calls⟩ ⟨114, 47, 130⟩ for Rustine versus ⟨974, 70, 372⟩ for RustMamp, while "Syzygy translations contain no unsafe constructs, compared to 14 in Rustine translations"
effect_correctness_headline: "Rustine can generate fully compilable Rust code for all and achieve 87% functional equivalence (passing 1,063,099 assertions out of 1,221,192 in test suites with average function and line coverage of 74.7% and 72.2%)" — 100% compilation is fully automated, while the 87% assertion pass rate includes a human developer repairing semantic mismatches in 4.5 hours on average; 10 of 23 projects reached 100% functional equivalence with no human intervention
notes: Dimension mapping is a judgment call a human reviewer should confirm: the paper's 'safety' metrics (raw pointer declarations/dereferences, pointer arithmetic/comparisons, unsafe lines/casts/calls) are memory-safety proxies and were coded as the security dimension, while 'idiomaticity' (Clippy flags per normalized KLoC) and the three readability metrics were coded as readability-maintainability. Tables 1, 2 and 3 and Figures 6, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 14 are badly garbled by PDF extraction (column values appear as long interleaved runs of numbers), so only the aggregate figures quoted in the running text were copied; per-project values must be re-checked against the PDF. The paper also reports a human study, but it measures repair effort rather than rating code quality: one developer with over ten years of C and Rust experience and no familiarity with the subjects repaired the non-equivalent translations in 4.5 hours on average (min 0.33, max 10), with a strong size-effort correlation (rho = 0.86, p = 1.59e-4); there is a single annotator and no agreement statistic, which is why human_eval is coded 'none'. Statistical tests are reported only for effort/cost/time correlations, not for the quality metrics, and each project appears to be translated once with no repeated runs or variance. The reported 87% functional equivalence is not fully automated. Contamination of the open-source C subjects in the models' pretraining is never discussed. A_max and the block threshold theta_b are not given numerically (theta_f is 50% of the LLM context window). The authors note they recalculated several baselines' metrics after finding bugs or suppressed Clippy rules in those artifacts, which makes the baseline numbers theirs rather than as-published.
family_reason: The safety gains come mainly from pre-translation C refactoring (pointer arithmetic to indexing, constness, unary desugaring) plus dependency and API context injected into the translation prompt; the ablation removing refactoring sharply raises unsafe constructs, while the compiler-feedback loop mainly secures compilability.
scope_reason: Outcome is the memory-safety, idiomaticity and readability of LLM-generated Rust translations.
gain_metric: number of unsafe lines in the Rust translation of bzip2 (rustc_hir count)
gain_quote:
in Rustine translations (⟨114, 47, 130⟩) are notably less compared to RustMamp
(⟨974, 70, 372⟩)
gain_note: Per-project comparison on bzip2 (Table 3, row 21: unsafe lines/type casts/calls 114/47/130 vs 974/70/372). RustMamp and Syzygy are the strongest (LLM-based) baselines but each covers only one project; Syzygy has zero unsafe constructs on zopfli versus 14 for Rustine, so Rustine does not win on every project. Transpiler baselines (C2Rust, C2SaferRust, CROWN, Laertes) are much worse across overlapping projects. The text claim that RustMamp has 69 vs Rustine 20 pointer arithmetic on bzip2 (ID=22) does not match Table 3 (69 and 20 there are dereference counts), a minor internal inconsistency.
core_idea: Repository-level C-to-Rust translation that preprocesses and refactors C (pointer arithmetic to array indexing, constness maximization, unary desugaring, function breakdown), builds a dependence graph to order translation and supply context, and translates with a two-tier LLM loop using compiler feedback and adaptive in-context examples.
core_idea_checked: Five stages: C preprocessing, semantics-preserving refactoring checked by tests, dependence-graph construction with RAG-style API descriptions and FFI suggestions, reverse-topological translation with DeepSeek-V3 then DeepSeek-R1 under compiler-error feedback and error-code-indexed in-context examples, and test-based validation with stack-trace-guided debugging.
note: Strong evaluation on 23 real C repositories, but the technique is tied to migrating existing C projects to Rust and cannot run on function-level generation benchmarks.

title: RepoOMP: Repository-Aware Hotspot OpenMP Parallelization via Dependency-Aware Context Reduction
technique_name: RepoOMP (MAP repository graph + Rule-Agent Router + Structured Transformation Context + verification/rollback loop)
metrics: efficiency: speedup over serial -O3 at 16 threads, five-run arithmetic mean, plus accepted-set median/IQR and thread/platform sweeps [execution]; cost: model-side tokens and wall-clock time; correctness: build failure / wrong answer under workload-specific oracles (MD5, PSNR, top-5 accuracy, energy drift) [execution]; ThreadSanitizer warning counts as supplementary audit
benchmarks: NPB 3.0 OpenMP C (8 kernels, Class A/B); BOTS (8 kernels); real-world repositories FFmpeg, NCNN, GROMACS (3 detailed kernels each; 951 profiled hotspots total, 330 accepted real-world hotspots)
models: GPT-5.1, size NR, closed, general/reasoning; Claude 4.5 Sonnet, size NR, closed, general; Gemini 3 Pro, size NR, closed, general/reasoning
baselines: Claude Code unstructured repository agent (same backbones, same 3-attempt budget, no MAP/STC); AutoPar (ROSE); Polly (LLVM); human-expert OpenMP versions; ablations No-Router, No-STC, Flat-Ctx, Rule-Only, Agent-Only
effect_target_headline: RepoOMP achieves average speedups of 8.23× on NPB and 8.96× on BOTS (Claude Code-based baseline 3.31× and 4.12×); nine real-world kernels: cross-backbone mean of 5.25×, improves speedup by 18–28% relative to the unstructured Claude Code baseline (4.17×)
effect_correctness_headline: RepoOMP records zero BF/WA cells in the reported task tables, whereas the ClaudeCode-based workflows incur 26 such cells
notes: Eligibility borderline on EC4/adjacent: the LLM edits existing human-written repository code (OpenMP insertion), but the LLM generates the transformation, so treated as LLM-edited code with an efficiency outcome; reviewer should confirm against the 'adjacent' side list. Stage is both pre-generation (MAP/STC context) and a post-generation verification loop; coded as pre-generation since context construction is the core contribution. Tables 6-11 garbled in extraction (columns interleaved); headline numbers taken from text. Token reduction 47-68% vs Claude Code. Released repo is a 'Simplified' version.
family_reason: The core contribution is recovering repository dependency evidence (MAP graph) and packaging it into a bounded Structured Transformation Context for the LLM; ablations show context construction drives accepted rate and speedup.
scope_reason: Outcome is the runtime speedup of LLM-edited code (OpenMP pragmas inserted into existing repositories), verified by compilation and workload checks.
gain_metric: mean speedup over serial -O3 at 16 threads on nine real-world kernels (FFmpeg, NCNN, GROMACS)
baseline_name: Claude Code unstructured repository agent (Claude 4.5 Sonnet, same retry budget)
gain_quote:
RepoOMP variants improve the average from the Claude Code baseline’s 4.17×
to 4.94–5.46×.
gain_note: Table 10/11 averages; 4.94 is RepoOMP with the matched Claude 4.5 backbone, 5.46 with Gemini 3 Pro, 5.34 with GPT-5.1. On NPB/BOTS RepoOMP averages 8.23/8.96 vs Claude Code 3.31/4.12 and human-expert versions 6.25/7.57. Minor internal inconsistencies: Table 13 and Table 18 give different per-kernel RepoOMP speedups (e.g., Deshake 2.02 vs 1.94, MobileNet 6.05 vs 5.65), and the failure totals in the text (115 or 123 compile failures, 157 or 212 rollbacks) differ between sections; none changes the headline direction.
core_idea: Builds a repository-level dependency and performance graph, routes each profiled hotspot to a rule engine, an LLM agent or a skip path by propagated risk, and gives the agent a compact structured context of dependency facts before inserting OpenMP directives, with compile/check/speedup verification and rollback.
core_idea_checked: MAP (repo/file/function nodes with call and read/write edges plus profiling data) feeds bottom-up blocker propagation; a deterministic three-way router sends high-confidence hotspots to rules, middle-confidence ones to an LLM with a five-field Structured Transformation Context, and skips low-confidence ones; each transformation is compiled, checked against workload oracles and timed, with rollback on failure.

title: TritonRL: Training LLMs to Think and Code Triton Without Cheating
technique_name: TritonRL: SFT distillation (DeepSeek-R1 or GPT-OSS 120B traces) + GRPO with Hierarchical Reward Decomposition (speedup reward on plan tokens, correctness reward on code tokens) gated by rule-based and LLM-judge validity verifiers

scope_reason: Outcome is the runtime speedup of LLM-generated Triton kernels over the PyTorch reference, gated by correctness and validity checks.

title: Xe-Forge: Multi-Stage LLM-Powered Kernel Optimization for Intel GPU
technique_name: Xe-Forge: LLM-planned multi-stage optimization pipeline with Chain-of-Verification-and-Refinement (CoVeR) agents and Intel GPU knowledge base
metrics: efficiency: speedup and TFLOPS vs PyTorch eager, torch.compile and unoptimized Triton; geometric mean speedup; fraction of kernels improving; roofline placement [execution]

baselines: PyTorch eager; torch.compile (TorchInductor); unoptimized KernelFalcon-generated Triton kernel (pipeline input)
effect_target_headline: 1.17× geometric mean speedup over PyTorch eager with 67% of kernels improving (97 Level-2 KernelBench kernels, Intel Arc Pro B70); 2–13.3× speedups on Flash Attention across all tested configurations without regression
effect_correctness_headline: Across all benchmarked kernels the pipeline maintains 100% correctness
notes: Input kernels are LLM-generated (KernelFalcon) correct Triton code, which the LLM pipeline then rewrites; treated as LLM generation/editing rather than refactoring human code. scope_reason: The outcome is the execution efficiency (speedup/TFLOPS) of Triton kernels that an LLM (KernelFalcon) generated and that the pipeline's LLM then rewrites.

core_idea: Optimization experience is stored in a two-level graph of coarse global optimization directions, fine-grained local strategy cards and directed transition edges; at each evolution step a deterministic feature-based score over recent-prefix transition edges picks the global direction, the LLM picks a local strategy under it, and execution feedback is written back into the nodes and edges.

title: Idioms: A Simple and Effective Framework for Turbo-Charging Local Neural Decompilation with Well-Defined Types
technique_name: IDIOMS (finetuning for joint prediction of code and user-defined type definitions, with breadth-first call-graph neighboring-function context, trained on the new REALTYPE dataset)
metrics: readability-maintainability (naming, type/structure documentation): variable name accuracy, variable type accuracy, UDT variable nominal accuracy, UDT variable structural accuracy, plus TypeForge-style composite data structure identification and struct layout recovery precision/recall/F1 [similarity-to-reference]; correctness co-outcome: passes EXEBENCH tests [execution] and relaxed/plain/strict dependency-equivalence via dependency-graph isomorphism [tool-static]

baselines: Nova (6.7b) and LLM4Decompile (6.7b) neural decompilers; standalone type recovery tools Retypd, BinSub, TRex and TypeForge; internal ablations: exebench training, parity-exebench (size-matched training set), functions-realtype (function-only context)
effect_target_headline: On EXEBENCH, IDIOMS vs LLM4Decompile vs Nova: variable name accuracy 20.6 / 14.7 / 12.9, variable type accuracy 58.2 / 45.5 / 41.8, UDT variable nominal accuracy 20.7 / 0.0 / 0.0, UDT variable structural accuracy 34.5 / 0.0 / 0.0; on REALTYPE at O0: 19.8 / 3.4 / 4.5, 38.3 / 13.4 / 13.0, 6.4 / 0.0 / 0.0 and 15.0 / 0.0 / 0.0 respectively (Nova and LLM4Decompile score 0 because they do not predict UDTs). title: AccelOpt: A Self-Improving LLM Agentic System for AI Accelerator Kernel Optimization
technique_name: AccelOpt (three-agent planner/executor/summarizer workflow + beam search over candidate kernels + self-curated optimization memory of slow-fast kernel pairs)
metrics: efficiency: percentage of peak throughput computed from a roofline model (min required HBM traffic / bandwidth, matmul FLOPs / PeakMM, vector FLOPs / PeakVec) over measured latency; measured kernel latency in ms (warm-up iterations plus 10 repeated runs, up to 10 rounds, 1% (Trainium 1) / 4% (Trainium 2) difference threshold); speedup over the baseline kernel (geometric mean of per-task best speedup); cumulative Fast@p; traffic efficiency and tensor/vector/scalar engine utilization from the profiler [execution and profiler]; correctness: output compared against a CPU full-precision reference under several random seeds with a per-task tolerance [execution]; cost in US dollars from input+output token counts
benchmarks: NKIBench (new): 14 NKI kernels from real-world LLM workloads (AdamW, Add+RMSNorm+Matmul, BatchMatmul, BatchMatmul+Softmax, Group Query Attention, LoRA, Mamba block, Matmul+Add+RMSNorm, Matmul, RMSNorm+Matmul, RoPE, SiLU, SwiGLU, Transpose+Matmul), evaluated on Trainium 1 and Trainium 2; additionally 24 Triton kernels from FlashInfer-Bench on H100 and one Conv2D kernel from a Stanford CS149 assignment
models: gpt-oss-120b, open, reasoning (medium reasoning effort; planner/summarizer in the main setting and best executor in the cost study); gpt-oss-20b, open, reasoning; Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct-FP8, open, code-specialized instruct (executor in the main setting); Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507, open, reasoning; Claude Sonnet 4, closed, thinking mode enabled
baselines: Repeated sampling with Claude Sonnet 4 (thinking mode); repeated sampling of the same agentic workflow; beam search without optimization memory; a Reflexion-style reflector workflow; Claude Sonnet 4 used inside AccelOpt; Neuron-compiler-generated (or hand-written/official-example) baseline kernels; human expert reference kernels from the NKI tutorial (Mamba) and nki-samples (RoPE)
effect_target_headline: boosting the average percentage of peak throughput from 49% to 61% on Trainium 1 and from 45% to 59% on Trainium 2 for NKIBench kernels; 'using open-source models, it matches the kernel improvements of Claude Sonnet 4 while being 26x cheaper'; best geometric-mean speedup 1.235x ($139.00) vs 1.137x ($178.37) for the Reflexion-style baseline and 1.222x ($5806.83) for repeated sampling, with the model ensemble reaching 1.246x ($470.66); vs human experts, Mamba improved from the 28.4% baseline to 54.6% of peak (1.04x the best expert 52.7%) and RoPE from 21.1% to 29.6% of peak (1.4x the human reference); on 24 FlashInfer-Bench Triton kernels (H100) 1.27x average speedup over the best Triton baselines with 3.19x peak speedup
notes: Correctness is enforced as a gate (only kernels passing the CPU-reference check are kept and reported), so no correctness rate is reported for comparison; effect_correctness is recorded as neutral on that basis. The appendix reports that gpt-oss models sometimes exploited the correctness checker (fake speedups by omitting computation in safe softmax), which the authors flag as a need for stronger equivalence checking. Record metadata gives year 2025 and venue arXiv.org; the paper itself carries the MLSys 2026 proceedings header, which is what is recorded here. All figures (6, 7, 9-18) are images and their numbers could not be extracted, so the headline figures come from the abstract and prose; Tables 1-6 extracted readably. No repeated end-to-end runs of the system per configuration and no statistical tests; no dedicated threats-to-validity section, though Section 4.3 analyses limitations.
family_reason: Profiler-measured latency drives beam search over candidate kernels (the ablation shows beam search, not memory, gives the main gain), with planner/executor/summarizer agents and an optimization memory on top.
scope_reason: Outcome is the runtime efficiency (latency, percentage of peak throughput) of LLM-generated NKI kernels, with correctness gated by a CPU reference check.
gain_metric: geometric-mean best speedup over the initial NKIBench kernels (Trainium 1)

gain_note: No single span holds both numbers: 1.235 ($139.00) is the gpt-oss-120b planner+executor row of Table 3 / Table 1; Claude repeated sampling reaches 1.222 at $5806.83 (strongest baseline). Reflexion-style baseline: 1.137 vs 1.235 ('1.137× speedup ($178.37) versus 1.235× ($139.00)'). title: Project-Level C-to-Rust Translation via Pointer Knowledge Graphs
technique_name: PtrTrans (C-Rust Pointer Knowledge Graph-guided project-level C-to-Rust translation: KG construction, KG-guided unit-by-unit translation in dependency order, and KG-guided incremental error correction)
metrics: readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): Lint Alert Count from Rust-Clippy, broken down into style, complexity, correctness and performance lints [tool-static]; security (memory safety): Unsafe Usage Count from Cargo-geiger (unsafe fn declarations, unsafe {} blocks, raw pointer dereferences) [tool-static]; correctness: %Compiled = compiledFunc/translatedFunc and %Equiv. = equivalentFunc/translatedFunc on manually constructed unit tests [execution]; case study: DSR@k and CodeBLEU for manual fixing effort [human / similarity-to-reference]; efficiency: runtime of four correctly translated Rust projects vs their C versions [execution]
benchmarks: 16 real-world C projects from the Crown dataset (avl, buffer, genann, quadtree, rgba, urlparser, ht, bst, json.h, libtree, binn, bzip2, heman, libzahl, lil, lodepng), up to 14,829 LOC; unit tests built with LLM-generated harnesses plus AFL++ fuzzing achieve 80.0-97.7% line coverage and 87.7-100.0% function coverage

baselines: Crown (rule-based ownership-guided rewriting of c2rust output); PR2 (LLM-based rewriting of c2rust output); FLOURINE (fuzzing-enhanced LLM translation, bottom-up order, Restart repair strategy, same backbone LLM); ablations PtrTrans_PS (no pointer semantics, i.e. the conventional bottom-up call-graph paradigm), PtrTrans_PU (no pointer-usage information), PtrTrans_RA (no Rust-oriented annotations), PtrTrans_EC (no error correction)
effect_target_headline: Across the 16 projects, PtrTrans reduces the Lint Alert Count by 94.9% compared to Crown (from 6,802 to 349) and by 91.6% compared to PR2 (from 4,135 to 349). Similarly, PtrTrans reduces the Unsafe Usage Count by 99.9% against both Crown (from 141,866 to 85) and PR2 (from 134,185 to 85). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show both reductions are significant (p < 0.001); zero unsafe usages for projects under 4k LOC
effect_correctness_headline: For projects with LoC < 4K: average %Compiled 98.3 vs 69.9 and %Equiv. 81.6 vs 52.3 for FLOURINE (improvements of 28.4% and 29.3%); for 4K < LoC < 15K: %Compiled from 64.0% to 85.9% and functional equivalence from 14.2% to 67.9%. Efficiency is touched only in the threats-to-validity section: runtime of four correctly translated projects (avl, rgba, ht, bst) showed no degradation, with one figure given ('the translated Rust project runs 54% faster than the C version for the project bst'); no systematic efficiency evaluation. A human reviewer should check the fairness of the idiomaticity comparison: Crown and PR2 rewrite c2rust output for the whole project (hence enormous unsafe counts), while PtrTrans's counts are over its own translated project, which can contain unimplemented!() stubs for functions whose repair exhausted the five attempts (%Compiled below 100 for several projects). Record metadata gives year 2025 (arXiv v3 posted May 2026); the paper itself is Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, FSE, Article FSE162, July 2026, which is what is recorded. Table 3 and Table 6/7 are heavily garbled by the PDF extraction (column blocks separated from headers); the totals cited here were cross-checked against the prose and the per-category totals (style 2790/3808/233, complexity 3945/269/94, correctness 58/58/10, performance 9/0/12). No compute or cost reporting; no contamination discussion.
family_reason: The core mechanism is retrieving per-unit pointer semantics (usage information and ownership/mutability/lifetime annotations) from a statically built C-Rust pointer knowledge graph into the translation and repair prompts; compiler-driven repair mainly serves compilability.
scope_reason: Outcomes are unsafe-code usage (memory safety) and Clippy lint alerts (idiomaticity) of LLM-translated Rust code.

title: Ave: Guiding Agentic GPU Optimization Using Data-Flow Invariants

title: C2SaferRust: Transforming C Projects Into Safer Rust With NeuroSymbolic Techniques
technique_name: C2SaferRust (C2Rust transpilation + static-analysis-based decomposition into translation units with call-site/dataflow context + LLM translation to safe Rust + compiler/test feedback repair)
metrics: security/idiomaticity: raw pointer declarations, raw pointer dereferences, lines of unsafe code, unsafe call expressions, unsafe type casts (tool-static, counts via compiler analysis; metrics from Laertes prior work); correctness: end-to-end test pass, translation success rate (execution)
benchmarks: 7 GNU coreutils programs (split, pwd, cat, truncate, uniq, tail, head) with end-to-end tests (new benchmark); 10 of 17 Laertes benchmarks (no tests)
models: gpt-4o-mini, closed, instruct
baselines: C2Rust output (no technique); Laertes; CROWN (CROWN ran on 4 of 10 programs); ablations: No Chunking, Random Order; variant with direct C-to-Rust translation
effect_target_headline: we are able to reduce the number of raw pointers by up to 38%, and reduce the amount of unsafe code by up to 28% (coreutils benchmark); C2SaferRust outperforms other approaches with a 39/2/9 aggregate win/tie/loss record over all 5 metrics (Laertes benchmark)
effect_correctness_headline: The resulting programs still pass all test cases.
notes: Venue taken from metadata (IEEE TSE); full text is arXiv v2 and does not state the venue. Input to the LLM is machine-transpiled (C2Rust) code from human-written C, so it is LLM translation/editing rather than pure refactoring of human code; reviewer may check EC4 borderline. Safety metrics are custom static counts of unsafe constructs, framed as both safety and idiomaticity; mapping to 'security' is approximate (no CWE/vulnerability scan). Tables 2-5 are heavily garbled in extraction. Correctness is maintained by construction (failed units reverted); per-baseline correctness not reported. Single model (gpt4o-mini), no repeated runs.
family_reason: The safety gain comes from LLM translation prompts built from static-analysis slices (unit code, call sites, live-in/out variables, globals, imports) over callee-first ordered units; the compile/test repair loop mainly protects correctness, reverting failed units.
scope_reason: Outcome is the safety (unsafe code, raw pointers) of LLM-edited Rust produced from C2Rust output.
gain_metric: Lines of unsafe code in the uniq program (coreutils), count
baseline_name: C2Rust transpiler output (no technique; Laertes and CROWN could not run on the coreutils benchmark)
gain_quote: the largest reduction of 28%, highlighting C2S AFER R UST’s
gain_note: Table 2a, uniq, unsafe lines 6066 -> 4397 (28%); averages over 7 coreutils programs: raw pointer declarations -25%, dereferences -22%, unsafe lines -24%, unsafe calls -8%, unsafe casts -30%. All end-to-end tests still pass. On 10 Laertes programs (no tests) vs Laertes and CROWN: aggregate win/tie/loss 39/2/9 over 5 metrics (Table 3). Single run, gpt-4o-mini, N=5 repair attempts, L=150.
core_idea: Transpile C with C2Rust, decompose the unsafe Rust into small translation units ordered callee-first, prompt an LLM to rewrite each unit into safe idiomatic Rust with static-analysis context, and keep a unit only if the program compiles and passes end-to-end tests after up to N feedback repairs.
core_idea_checked: C2Rust output is split by an AST traversal into units of at most L lines, ordered by reverse topological call-graph order; each unit plus call sites or live-in/live-out variables, globals and imports is sent to gpt-4o-mini to convert to idiomatic Rust, swapped in, compiled and tested, with compiler/test feedback for up to N attempts, otherwise reverted.
note: Project-level C-to-Rust migration technique; it needs a C project, C2Rust and end-to-end tests, so it cannot run on function-level generation benchmarks.

title: A Preliminary Study on the Robustness of Code Generation by Large Language Models
technique_name: RobGen (line-level intervention checker + token-level conditional logit adjustment of the 'if' token)

benchmarks: CoderEval Java, 230 repository-level tasks
models: DeepSeekCoder-1.3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; StarCoder2-7B, open, code-specialized

effect_target_headline: RobGen reduces the proportion of less robust code by 10% (across five models); e.g., DeepSeekCoder-1.3B generated code underperforming human drops from 42.2% to 28.7%; average AvgABE 2.42 vs 1.65 greedy
effect_correctness_headline: achieves the highest average Pass@1 (43.57) vs 42.09 for greedy sampling
notes: Borderline on NF dimension: the target is 'robustness' (defensive programming: missing null/range/value checks, error handling), not explicitly security (no CWE/vulnerability scanner); mapped to security as input-validation-related; reviewer should decide whether robustness counts as an eligible NF dimension. The LLM judge was validated against manual comparison on 100 pairs (kappa 0.81) in the empirical part, and the open-coding of robustness patterns had kappa 0.71 between two authors. Judge scores averaged over 3 runs; runtime averaged over 3 runs on 20 tasks (RobGen +33.4% for DSC-1.3B, up to +197.9% for QWC-1.5B). Table 3 extraction is garbled but recoverable. Higher AvgABE is not monotonically better (StarCoder2-7B w/o checker 7.76 = redundant ifs).
family_reason: A line-level checker (LoRA-tuned Qwen3-0.6B) triggers a logit boost of the 'if' token during greedy decoding; no retraining of the generator.
scope_reason: Outcome is the robustness (defensive programming: input validation, boundary checks, error handling) of LLM-generated Java code, mapped to security; borderline because no vulnerability scanner or CWE metric is used.
gain_metric: Share of generated code judged less robust than the human reference by GPT-4o pairwise comparison (DeepSeekCoder-1.3B), %
gain_quote: for DeepSeekCoder-1.3B drops from 42.2% to 28.7%
gain_note: Section 4.1.2 text; per-method judge results for RobustCoder Prompt and Post-Generation Insertion appear only in Figure 9 without numbers. Table 3 average AvgABE (atomic boolean expressions, a gameable proxy): greedy 1.65, RobustCoder Prompt 1.73, PGI 2.06, RobGen 2.42 (w/o checker 3.41); average Pass@1 greedy 42.09, RobGen 43.57. Abstract headline: 'reduces the proportion of less robust code by 10%' across five models. CoderEval Java, 230 tasks, single greedy run; judge kappa 0.81 on 100 pairs.
core_idea: During decoding, a small trained checker decides at each new line whether a conditional is needed and, if so, boosts the logit of the 'if' token when it is already in the top three, so the model inserts missing guard checks.
core_idea_checked: RobGen: a LoRA-SFT Qwen3-0.6B classifier trained on 12,000 GitHub Java blocks predicts whether the next line starts with 'if'; when positive and 'if' ranks within the top three, its logit is raised by delta*(rank-1) via a LogitsProcessor, with delta set to the 90th percentile of observed logit gaps per model.
note: Half of the paper is an empirical robustness study, but RobGen is a reusable model-agnostic decoding plug-in with its own baselines and ablation; needs open-weight logits access.

title: SpecGen: Accelerating Agentic Kernel Optimization with Speculative Generation

raising the final speedup from 5.05×

core_idea: A waterfall-style prompt chain for geospatial code with a shared JSON information pool, geospatial knowledge-base retrieval, human-feedback debugging loop, and a final code-commenting stage.
core_idea_checked: Section 3.1: requirement analysis to a JSON spec (8 elements), algorithm design into modules, implementation with retrieval from platform, function-syntax and dataset knowledge bases, up to 3 debugging rounds driven by user executability/accuracy feedback, then a commenting stage adding header metadata and per-module comments.
note: Domain-specific (GEE/geospatial knowledge bases, GeoCode-Eval) with human-in-the-loop debugging; readability is a side metric of a hallucination/executability paper and several reported numbers are inconsistent with the tables.

title: Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators
technique_name: ZOMBOSS: compiler-mediated agentic mapping search (LLM agent selects/constrains typed mapping decisions; generated ACT backend completes, legalizes and emits native code; feedback from verified correctness and measured cycles)
metrics: efficiency: kernel cycle count measured on FPGA (Gemmini) and simulator latency (PLENA), geometric-mean speedup [execution]; correctness: full-output numerical verification against an oracle, coverage of instances with a correct kernel
benchmarks: KernelCraft benchmark definitions and input shapes: 20 Gemmini instances (BatchMatMul, GEMM, GEMV, Linear) and 36 PLENA instances (12 families incl. FFN, FlashAttn, GEMM, GEMV, GQA, MHA, MQA, SwiGLU, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, SiLU, Softmax)
models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, closed (API), instruct; DeepSeek-V4-Pro, closed (API), instruct (ablation only)
baselines: Neural: direct agentic native-kernel generation following KernelCraft; Candidate-0: compiler default mapping; random sampling over the legal catalog
effect_target_headline: geometric-mean speedups of 3.34× on Gemmini and 1.10× on PLENA relative to the compiler default; 1.79× geometric-mean speedup over Neural's best correct kernel in each of Neural's 14 successful Gemmini runs; on PLENA's 12 Neural-success instances Neural is 1.02× faster in geometric mean
effect_correctness_headline: correct verified kernel on 20/20 Gemmini and 36/36 PLENA instances; Neural succeeds on only 14/20 (70.0%) and 12/36 (33.3%)
notes: Borderline IC2: in ZOMBOSS the LLM outputs mapping decisions and the compiler backend emits the native code, so the final code is LLM-guided rather than LLM-written; the direct-generation baseline is LLM-written. The efficiency gain over the compiler default comes from LLM-guided search; vs. direct LLM generation it is mixed (better on Gemmini, slightly worse on PLENA where both succeed). PLENA results take the best of three runs. Also reports 71.2%/54.2% token reductions vs. Neural. Figures with per-instance results are garbled.
family_reason: An LLM agent iteratively proposes mapping decisions and is steered by verified correctness and measured cycle feedback; the compiler backend completes and emits the code.
scope_reason: The LLM chooses mapping decisions and a generated compiler backend writes the native kernel, so the final code is LLM-guided rather than LLM-written; the comparison baseline is LLM-written.
gain_metric: geometric-mean kernel speedup (FPGA-measured cycles) over Neural's best correct kernel on the 14 Gemmini instances where Neural succeeded
baseline_name: Neural (direct agentic native-kernel generation following KernelCraft, DeepSeek-V4-Flash)
gain_quote: a 1.79× geometric-mean speedup
gain_note: Section IV-B. Baseline value 1 is the normalized Neural reference (speedup ratio). Neural is conditioned on success (14/20). On PLENA, on the 12 Neural-success instances, Neural is 1.02x faster in geometric mean. Against the compiler default (Candidate-0) ZOMBOSS reaches 3.34x (Gemmini) and 1.10x (PLENA). PLENA reports the best of three search runs; Gemmini single run.
core_idea: Place the LLM agent above an automatically generated accelerator compiler backend: the agent selects or constrains typed mapping decisions, the backend legalizes, completes and emits native code, and verified cycle feedback drives the search.
core_idea_checked: Algorithm 1: compiler generates a workload mapping surface and default plan; each iteration the agent proposes an intent (catalog pick on Gemmini, hard/preferred/auto region on PLENA), ACT completes and legalizes it into plans, code is generated, verified against an oracle and timed, and only verified improvements replace the incumbent.
note: Tensor-accelerator (Gemmini FPGA, PLENA simulator) kernel mapping search that depends on a TAIDL/ACT-generated backend; not applicable to general function-level benchmarks.

One application (tennis court booking API), one model (GPT-5.3-Codex in OpenCode), three runs per condition ({50,50,48} vs {42,43,42}). title: KernelBand: Steering LLM-based Kernel Optimization via Hardware-Aware Multi-Armed Bandits
technique_name: KernelBand (hardware-aware masked UCB contextual bandit over kernel clusters x optimization strategies, with profiling-based pruning and trace-driven clustering)
metrics: efficiency: geometric mean speedup over reference kernel and Fast@1 (% tasks with speedup >1.0x) [execution]; correctness: Correct (%) via call accuracy and execution accuracy (torch.allclose) [execution]
benchmarks: TritonBench-G (corrected GEAK version), 183 kernels after excluding sin_computation (13 categories, 5 difficulty levels); 50-kernel stratified subset for analyses; 30-kernel subset for PyTorch comparison
models: DeepSeek-V3.2, size NR, open-weights, instruct (primary); GPT-5, closed, NR; Claude Opus 4.5, closed, NR; Gemini 3 Flash, closed, NR
baselines: GEAK (Reflexion-style Triton kernel agent); Best-of-N sampling (N=T); PyTorch eager, torch.compile inductor, torch.compile max-autotune; ablations incl. LLM strategy selection, w/o strategy set
effect_target_headline: On A100, KernelBand attains 1.91× geometric mean speedup with 79.8% correctness, outperforming the best performing baseline, GEAK, by 42.5% in speedup (GEAK 1.34×, BoN 0.98×); RTX 4090 1.74× vs. 1.44×; H20 1.45× vs. 1.06×
effect_correctness_headline: A100 Correct (All): KernelBand 79.8 vs GEAK 48.0 vs BoN 31.2; H20: 79.3 vs 49.4 vs 29.3; RTX 4090: 77.8 vs 55.6 vs 31.1
notes: Arxiv v2 Feb 2026 though metadata year 2025. Tables extracted with garbled layout but readable. Single run per configuration; median timing per shape but no variance across runs. Cost analysis: $0.50 per kernel budget yields 1.83x vs GEAK 1.35x, BoN 1.22x. No code URL, no threats-to-validity section. GPU kernel optimization is efficiency-only; code is LLM-rewritten from a reference kernel.
family_reason: A hardware-aware masked UCB bandit picks (kernel cluster, optimization strategy) pairs and updates from measured speedups of LLM-rewritten kernels, an execution-feedback search loop.
scope_reason: Outcome is runtime speedup of LLM-generated Triton kernels with correctness checked by allclose.
gain_metric: geometric-mean speedup over the reference kernel on TritonBench-G (all levels, correct tasks only), H20
gain_note: Section 4.2 / Table 1, DeepSeek-V3.2, T=20. Headline on A100 is 1.91x vs GEAK 1.34x and RTX 4090 1.74x vs 1.44x. Standard-mode geometric mean averages only correct tasks, and KernelBand also has much higher correctness (79.3% vs 49.4% on H20). Single run per configuration.
core_idea: Treat LLM kernel optimization as a contextual multi-armed bandit over (runtime-behavior cluster, optimization strategy) arms, pruning strategies that target already saturated hardware resources from Nsight profiling and selecting with masked UCB.
core_idea_checked: Algorithm 1: maintain a frontier of valid kernels, K-means cluster them every 10 iterations on a 5-d runtime feature vector, profile cluster centroids with NCU, mask strategies whose target resource exceeds 75% saturation, choose (cluster, strategy) by masked UCB, sample a kernel by headroom, have the LLM apply the strategy, verify and update reward with relative latency improvement.
note: GPU Triton kernel optimization over 183 TritonBench-G kernels on three GPUs and four LLMs; strong gains but tied to GPU kernels and no released code.

title: ChipMEM: Verification-Grounded Memory for EDA Agents
technique_name: ChipMEM (verification-gated procedural skill memory retrieved by RTL embedding similarity + hierarchical Beta statistical memory for tool retry/recovery advice)
metrics: efficiency: mean area improvement (%), power improvement (%), timing/WNS/TNS change, cell/wire ratio after synthesis [execution/tool synthesis measurements]; correctness: functional equivalence pass rate, strict gate pass rate, CVDP hidden-test pass rate [execution/formal]
benchmarks: RTL-OPT (38 designs); RTLRewriter-Bench (59 cases: 54 short, 5 long; 54 scored); custom open-source design set (20 designs); OpenTitan (10 IP blocks x 5 attempts); held-out cohorts A (20) and B (16); CVDP CID012/CID013 (40 testbench tasks); SWE-bench Pro pilot (100 tasks)
models: GPT-5.5, size NR, closed, reasoning (medium); Qwen3.8-27B, 27B, open, NR
baselines: Same EDA agent with memory disabled; procedural-only and Bayesian-only ablations; RTL-OPT reported results for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek R1; SWE-agent baseline in pilot
effect_target_headline: on the 49-design short suite, mean area improvement is 8.69% versus 5.66%; RTL-OPT mean area improvement from 6.18% to 8.79%; OpenTitan mean area and power improvement from 0.05%/0.00% to 0.24%/2.54%
effect_correctness_headline: On RTLRewriter-Bench, ChipMEM produces equivalence-passing outputs on 39/54 scored designs versus 35/54 without memory; OpenTitan full-PPA gate passes rise from 1/10 to 4/10 with equivalence maintained at 6/10
notes: Domain is hardware RTL PPA (area/power/timing) rather than software runtime; reviewer should confirm RTL PPA counts as efficiency. CVDP testbench part is test code (EC3-type) and not used for the NF outcome. GPT-5.5 experiments run on proprietary Cadence ChipStack 2.0 agent (limits reimplementation). RTL-OPT ChipMEM result selects best valid result across three result sets (favourable selection). Custom-design Pass@k is lower with ChipMEM (80% vs 85% at Pass@5). Appendix notes the legacy OpenTitan run mined skills after every session including failures, not the PASS-only rule. Held-out transfer only on CVDP (testbench) tasks with frozen memory; held-out PPA cohorts had no memory-off comparison. Mean ± std and bootstrap CIs for cost; no significance tests on PPA. Tables garbled but recoverable. Dated year 2026 (arXiv 2609.27067).
family_reason: Most of the work is done by a verification-gated procedural skill library retrieved by RTL-embedding similarity; the Bayesian retry/recovery memory is a secondary within-session aid.
scope_reason: Outcome is synthesized area/power (hardware resource efficiency) of LLM-agent-edited RTL code; counts as EFF only if hardware PPA is accepted as efficiency.
gain_metric: mean post-synthesis area improvement (%) on RTLRewriter-Bench 49-design short suite
baseline_name: Same EDA agent (Cadence ChipStack 2.0, GPT-5.5) with memory disabled
gain_quote: mean area improvement is 8.69% versus 5.66%
gain_note: Abstract and Table 3(b). Other settings: RTL-OPT 6.18 -> 8.79 (best valid result across three result sets, favourable selection); OpenTitan area/power 0.05/0.00 -> 0.24/2.54 (Qwen3.8-27B); custom set 0.14/0.39 -> 0.31/0.52. Memory-off is the only matched baseline; earlier RTL-OPT numbers for GPT-4o/DeepSeek R1 (max 4.80) use other models. Single run per setting, no significance tests on PPA; custom-design Pass@5 lower with memory (80 vs 85).
core_idea: Give an EDA agent a memory layer that stores LLM-distilled skills only from tool-verified passing sessions, retrieves them for new designs by RTL embedding similarity, and adds hierarchical Beta statistics over tool-call outcomes to advise retries and recovery strategies.
core_idea_checked: Procedural memory keyed by task (top RTL file) embeddings, top-2 retrieval at cosine threshold 0.6, skills added only after verified PASS; statistical memory = hierarchical Beta retry predictor and recovery ranking that triggers an LLM recovery planner below 0.20 success probability.
note: RTL PPA optimization tied to EDA toolchains (Yosys/ABC/OpenROAD, proprietary ChipStack agent); the SWE-bench Pro pilot measures resolve rate only, not NF quality.

title: EvolVE: Evolutionary Search for LLM-based Verilog Generation and Optimization
technique_name: EvolVE Idea-Guided Refinement (IGR): LLM idea generation (optionally RAG over papers) followed by diff-based sequential refinement chains scored by testbench pass and Area x Latency product
metrics: efficiency: area (um2), latency (cycles x clock period), power (mW), Area-Latency (AT) product and PPA product improvement ratio vs. human reference, swept over clock periods 3-7 ns [execution / commercial synthesis tool]; correctness: testbench pass rate, Pass@nodes on VerilogEval v2, Mod-VerilogEval v2, RTLLM v2 [execution]
benchmarks: IC-RTL (6 problems: LBP, GEMM, CONV, JAM, Huffman Coding, Distance Transform; from Taiwan National IC Design Contest and hand-crafted) for PPA; VerilogEval v2 spec-to-rtl (156), Mod-VerilogEval v2, RTLLM v2 (50) for correctness
models: DeepSeek-R1-FP4, 671B MoE, open, reasoning (used for PPA); GPT-OSS-120B, 120B, open, reasoning; Siliconmind-7B, 7B, open, code-specialized (SFT+GRPO); Gemini-2.0-Flash, size NR, closed, instruct
baselines: PPA: human-authored contest reference implementations (initial code); Dolphin's program on GEMM. Correctness: repeated sampling baselines per model, REvolution, VerilogCoder
effect_target_headline: reducing the Power, Performance, Area (PPA) product by up to 66% in Huffman Coding and 17% in the geometric mean across all problems (IC-RTL, IGR with DeepSeek-R1-FP4, Synopsys DC TSMC 180nm)
effect_correctness_headline: DeepSeek-R1-FP4-MCTS achieves peak pass rates of 98.1% on VerilogEval v2 and 92.0% on RTLLM v2 (300 nodes; baseline 95.5% and 86.0%)
notes: Domain is hardware RTL PPA; reviewer should confirm it counts as efficiency. MCTS variant evaluated for correctness only (not an NF technique). PPA results only for IGR with DeepSeek-R1-FP4 on 6 problems, compared to human reference designs (no LLM-baseline PPA comparison except Dolphin on GEMM); Q1 converged to baseline, Q3 had power regression (0.45 mW to 0.50 mW) neutralizing PPA gain. Prompt-steered Opt Area / Opt Cycle variants also reported. Single runs, no variance. STG token reduction (38,818 to 15,440 output tokens for DeepSeek-R1-FP4) reported. Only IC-RTL benchmark released; codebase 'will be released shortly'. Appendix D tables heavily garbled.
family_reason: IGR is an evolutionary search where testbench pass and synthesized Area x Latency scores drive diff-based refinement chains; idea generation/RAG only seeds the chains.
scope_reason: Outcome is the PPA (area, latency, power) of LLM-generated Verilog, a hardware efficiency property of generated code.
gain_metric: geometric-mean PPA-product reduction vs human contest reference designs on IC-RTL (%)
gain_quote: product by up to 66% in Huffman Coding and 17% in the geometric mean across all problems
gain_note: Abstract; Figure 5 ratios with Appendix D tables (heavily garbled). Baseline is the human reference normalized as zero reduction; no LLM baseline PPA except Dolphin on GEMM (Table 2: AT 330119680 vs initial 390463336). Only 6 problems, IGR with DeepSeek-R1-FP4 only, single runs; Q1 converged to baseline and Q3 power regression neutralized PPA gain.
core_idea: Generate diverse architectural ideas with an LLM (optionally RAG over papers) and refine each through a chain of diff-based edits scored by testbench pass and synthesized Area x Latency, keeping the best design.
core_idea_checked: IGR: k=60 ideas x m=5 Aider-style diff refinement steps (300 nodes), score -A*L/eta when all tests pass else penalty, STG testbenches for fine-grained feedback; MCTS variant used for correctness only.
note: Only the IC-RTL benchmark is public; the EvolVE codebase is stated to be released later.

title: MoTCoder: Elevating Large Language Models with Modular of Thought for Challenging Programming Tasks
technique_name: Module-of-Thought (MoT) instruction tuning (GPT-4o-transformed modular solutions with sub-module headers/docstrings, plus 'clean' renamed/commented code, filtered by tests)
metrics: readability-maintainability: Maintainability Index (Halstead volume, cyclomatic complexity, LOC, comment density) via radon on passing code [tool-static]; efficiency: average execution time (s) and memory usage (MB) on passing samples [execution]; correctness: pass@1 [execution]
benchmarks: APPS test set (introductory/interview/competition); CodeContests test and validation; training data from APPS and CodeContests train (183K clean + 174K MoT samples)
models: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, 7B, open, code-specialized instruct (base for MoTCoder-7B); Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, 32B, open, code-specialized instruct (base for MoTCoder-32B)
baselines: Base Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct; normal fine-tuning on original training solutions; many prior code LLMs (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, WizardCoder, StarCoder, GPT-4o) and code-revision methods (Self-edit, CodeRL, Self-repair, CodeChain)
effect_correctness_headline: APPS pass@1 All: MoTCoder-7B 34.67 vs Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct-7B 32.21 (normal finetuning 27.70); MoTCoder-32B 45.95 vs 40.13; CodeContests All: MoTCoder-7B 19.09, MoTCoder-32B 23.85
notes: Maintainability index and time/memory results are only shown in Figure 4 (b,c) with no printed numbers, so no exact NF headline can be copied; text states MoT code has 'significantly higher maintainability' than normal finetuning and baseline, and 'significantly lower memory consumption' with comparable time. NF metrics computed only on passing code (selection bias). Efficiency effect: memory lower, time comparable. Abstract pass@1 gains (5.8% APPS, 5.9% CodeContests) are relative to prior SOTA. Deduplication between CodeContests train and APPS test reported. No variance, no threats section, no compute reported. Text claims 'MoTCoder-6.7B outperformed GPT-4 by 12.61%' appears inconsistent with the current tables (stale from earlier version).
family_reason: Gains come from instruction tuning Qwen2.5-Coder on GPT-4o-transformed modular (sub-module header/docstring then implementation) solutions.
scope_reason: Paper measures the Maintainability Index (radon) and time/memory of code generated by the fine-tuned model.
gain_metric: average Maintainability Index (radon) of passing generated code
baseline_name: Normal fine-tuning on original APPS/CodeContests solutions (and base Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct)
gain_quote: higher maintainability compared to normal finetuning code
gain_note: MI and time/memory results appear only in Figure 4(b,c) with no printed numbers, so no numeric gain can be quoted. Text states MoT code has significantly higher MI than normal finetuning and baseline on all levels, and lower memory with comparable time. NF metrics only on passing code. Stale claim 'MoTCoder-6.7B outperformed GPT-4 by 12.61%' is inconsistent with current tables but concerns correctness, not the NF result.
core_idea: Fine-tune a code LLM on solutions rewritten into a two-step Module-of-Thought format (first sub-module headers with docstrings, then implementations combined into the final solution), plus cleaned renamed/commented code, filtered by tests.
core_idea_checked: GPT-4o transforms APPS/CodeContests training solutions into clean (174K/183K) and MoT data validated by tests; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/32B-Instruct are instruction-tuned one epoch on it.
note: General Python function-level generation; NF evidence is figure-only, which limits numeric comparison.

title: TRIM: Reducing AI-Generated CodeSlop via Agent Trajectory Minimization
technique_name: TRIM (Trajectory-guided Redundancy Identification and Minimization), hierarchical counterfactual patch minimization over agent repair trajectories (TRIM-G and TRIM-NG variants)
metrics: readability-maintainability: Delta Slop % = normalized reduction in patch length (modified lines), edits/hunks removed [tool-static]; verbosity removed per SlopCodeBench definition [tool-static]; correctness: Live-kBench oracle = crash-reproducing script + Gemini-3-Flash LLM judge of semantic equivalence to developer patch (9 judgments, majority vote) [execution + llm-judge]; SWE-Bench hidden fail-to-pass tests [execution]; cost = number of test-suite executions
benchmarks: Live-kBench (534 Linux kernel vulnerabilities; 433 repaired, 293 non-trivial evaluated); SWE-Bench-Verified (333 SWE-agent Claude-Sonnet-4 trajectories); 4,544 repair trajectories total
models: Gemini-3-Pro (closed); Claude-Opus-4.5 (closed); Claude-Sonnet-4 (closed); Gemini-3-Flash (closed, minimization baseline and judge); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed, minimization baseline)
baselines: Agentic minimization with mini-SWE-agent (Only Diff, Only Traj, Both prompts; Gemini-3-Flash and Sonnet 4.6); DD-Hunk (Delta Debugging adapted to patch hunks); original agent patch
effect_target_headline: TRIM cuts CODESLOP by 17.9%–32.9% across agentic scaffolds (Live-kBench, TRIM-G edit level); 1.6×–3.1× improvement over agentic minimization; 20.0% ∆Slop on SWE-Bench-Verified (modified files); 66% of AP-introduced verbosity removed
effect_correctness_headline: TRIM preserves oracle correctness for 327/330 (99.1%) successful repairs (SWE-Bench-Verified); Live-kBench CrashFixer 22.47% -> 23.41% (+0.94), OpenHands -1.13 under full minimization
notes: Technique is a deterministic post-processing algorithm (not an LLM call) applied to LLM-agent patches; eligibility hinges on accepting patch minimization of LLM-generated code as an NF (maintainability/redundancy) intervention. CodeSlop is a functional-redundancy (patch-length) metric defined by the authors, not an established maintainability metric; verbosity measured via SlopCodeBench definition. Live-kBench is a 'live' recent-bug benchmark (partial contamination handling). Statistical test only vs DD-Hunk (p = 0.50, 95% CI). Abstract says 17.9% while intro says 17.8%. Tables partially garbled. No artifact URL.
family_reason: TRIM is a test-validated counterfactual search that removes trajectory edit groups and keeps a removal only if the task test suite still passes.
scope_reason: Outcome is removable redundancy (patch size, verbosity) in LLM-agent-generated patches, a maintainability property of LLM-edited code.
gain_metric: Delta Slop: normalized reduction in patch length (%) on Live-kBench, CrashFixer trajectories
gain_quote: removing 32.9% versus 31.5% of C ODE S LOP
gain_note: Section VI RQ3 / Figure 5 (p = 0.50, statistically equivalent; TRIM needs about half the validations, 2.6k vs 5.2k). Against the best agentic minimization baseline the gain is larger (Table I, CrashFixer: 32.9 vs 10.5 Only Traj with Gemini-3-Flash; 1.6x-3.1x across scaffolds). SWE-Bench-Verified: 20.0% Delta Slop on modified files, 66% of introduced verbosity removed. CodeSlop is an author-defined patch-length metric.
core_idea: Replay a coding agent's repair trajectory and hierarchically try removing edit sequences, then files, then single edit actions, accepting each removal only if the task tests still pass and the patch shrinks.
core_idea_checked: Algorithm 1: coarse-to-fine reverse-order counterfactual removal over edit sequence, file, edit action; TRIM-G iterates to a one-minimal fixpoint, TRIM-NG does one pass; validation uses the agent's own test/repro script only.
note: Deterministic post-processing that needs an agent trajectory with test feedback; evaluated on kernel and repository repair, applicable to any iterative agent output but not tied to a narrow domain.

title: HLSmith: An Expert-Guided Agentic Framework for C/C++-to-HLS Translation
technique_name: HLSmith expert-guided agentic workflow: HLS optimization-expertise library of guarded transformation recipes (distilled from Rodinia-HLS) routed by bottleneck diagnosis, Translator/QoR Check/Optimizer/Orchestrator agents with Vitis tool feedback, flash vs multi-step modes, best-valid selection, and a hybrid early setup router
metrics: efficiency: HLS-synthesis estimated latency cycles and executed RTL co-simulation cycles, speedup over benchmark reference HLS and over expertise-off (geometric means, wins/losses) [execution / tool-static synthesis estimate]; correctness: C simulation vs CPU-golden outputs, RTL co-simulation pass, timing and resource fit [execution]
benchmarks: HLSFactory PolyBench kernels (28-kernel set; 26/27 used in sweeps); 14 kernels for ChatHLS comparison; 19 group-held-out kernels for router
models: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed); Claude Opus 4.8 (closed); GPT-5.5 (closed); DeepSeek V4 Flash (open); Grok 4.5 (closed); Gemma-4-31B (open, instruct); Qwen3.6-27B (open); Qwen3-0.6B (open, router)
baselines: ChatHLS; zero-shot generation; expertise-off agentic setups; benchmark reference HLS implementation; exhaustive setup selection (for router)
effect_target_headline: HLSmith achieves a geometric mean speedup of 4.24x over ChatHLS; On 8 common passes ... GM(LChatHLS /LHLSmith ) = 6.91×; Claude Sonnet 4.6: Bk /Sk is 17.46× versus Bk /Ok =6.07×; thus expertise adds 2.88× and wins 22/25 kernels against expertise off; up to 252× speedup over the reference HLS kernel
effect_correctness_headline: HLSmith reports 14 RTL co-simulation passes and ChatHLS 8 (14 kernels); functionally correct designs ... for every benchmark compared with a 57% valid-design rate of ChatHLS; Sonnet 4.6: All 154 completed agentic cells meet timing and resource limits, versus 18/26 zero-shot designs
notes: Efficiency here is hardware latency (HLS synthesis estimates / RTL co-simulation cycles) of generated FPGA designs; reviewer should confirm this counts as runtime efficiency. Abstract headline 4.24x is the sensitivity value excluding syr2k (6.91× on all 8 common passes). Several evaluations are small (4-5 kernels) and authors flag some as preliminary; Grok/DeepSeek RTL outputs not independently replayed. Figures 6-9 heavily garbled. Evaluation kernels excluded from adaptation training data (partial contamination handling). Source code listed as 'Pending'. No threats-to-validity section. Paper says token/time overhead is specified but only model-call counts appear in the text.
family_reason: Vitis C-sim/synthesis reports drive a staged diagnose-route-optimize-validate loop that keeps the best valid design; the routed expertise recipes are conditioned on that feedback.
scope_reason: Outcome is latency (synthesis-estimated and RTL co-simulation cycles) of LLM-generated HLS C/C++ accelerator code.
gain_metric: geometric-mean RTL co-simulation latency ratio L_ChatHLS / L_HLSmith on 8 common passes (x)
gain_quote: favors our HLSmith and GM(LChatHLS /LHLSmith ) = 6.91×.
gain_note: Section V-B / Fig. 8, 14 kernels attempted by both, HLSmith 14 RTL passes vs ChatHLS 8; baseline value 1 = ChatHLS latency normalized. Abstract headline 4.24x is the sensitivity value excluding syr2k. Internal ablation (Table V, Sonnet 4.6): Bk/Sk 17.46x vs expertise-off 6.07x (2.88x, 22/25 wins). scope_reason: The outcome is the execution efficiency (and correctness) of NPU kernel code that the LLM agent generates.

achieves a higher average Acc (0.80) and a faster average
execution Speedup (1.34×) across the evaluated L1 operators, significantly outperforming the strongest baseline,

core_idea: A training-free agent keeps a knowledge base of NPU kernel lessons stored as index tags plus a plain-language rationale plus a verified code snippet, retrieves entries by fusing exact-keyword and hardware-semantic rankings, and prunes or merges entries based on what actually compiled and ran.
core_idea_checked: Verified in Sections V-VII: Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation (metadata, rationale, artifact code) captured at run time under four trigger conditions, BM25 plus dense-embedding retrieval fused by reciprocal rank fusion with k=60 and K=6 entries per iteration, and an effect-driven distillation stage with validation, arbitration and merger sub-agents.

title: Beyond Correctness: Enhancing Architectural Reasoning in Code LLMs via Scalable Labeling with Agentic Judgment
technique_name: Agentic architectural judging pipeline for SFT data curation (Architecture Complexity Judge + Architecture Quality Judge with repository-specific generated rubrics), followed by supervised fine-tuning on the filtered trajectories
metrics: readability-maintainability (architectural conformance / structural quality): distribution of AQJ four-tier verdicts over all generated patches - High, High-with-concerns (HWC), Acceptable, Low - produced by a repository- and issue-specific rubric with priority-ordered axes and prose anchors [llm-judge]; the ACJ five-level complexity verdict (Trivial/Low/Moderate/High/Expert over five axes) is used for data selection, not as an outcome [llm-judge]. correctness: SWE-bench resolved rate under pass@1 (all specified unit tests pass on first attempt) [execution]; patch precision = resolved issues / patches generated [execution]. Convergent validity: Spearman correlation of the judge verdicts against 157 static architecture metrics [tool-static].
benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (500 verified bug-fixing instances) and SWE-bench Multilingual (300 bug-fixing instances across 9 non-Python languages). Training pool: 5,000 high-quality Python trajectories from RepoForge, filtered to 3,360 architecturally curated instances; the metric-based filtering baseline yields 1,548 instances. Stated to have no overlap between training and evaluation data.
models: Fine-tuned: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B (open-weights, instruct/reasoning). Teacher for trajectory generation: MiniMax-M2.5 (open-weights). Judge backbone: described only as 'a strong LLM' and never identified.
baselines: Original (base model, no fine-tuning); FullData (fine-tuned on the entire 5,000-trajectory pool, i.e. unfiltered SFT); Metrics (filtering by thresholded static architecture metrics, Qwen3-8B only); for the judge itself, random-forest prediction of ACJ/AQJ verdicts from 157 static metrics.
effect_target_headline: "our approach increases the proportion of architecturally conformant patches from 61-72% to 84-94% across model sizes" (abstract/introduction); per model, "For Qwen3-8B, the combined High+HWC proportion increases from 60.9% to 83.6%; for Qwen3-14B, from 64.0% to 87.1%; and for Qwen3-32B, from 72.1% to 93.5%." Versus the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural quality is only comparable: "High+HWC proportions of 83.6% vs. 87.5% on Qwen3-8B, 87.1% vs. 83.9% on Qwen3-14B, and 93.5% vs. 93.3% on Qwen3-32B".
effect_correctness_headline: "Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B/14B/32B on 3,360 curated instances achieves resolved rates of up to 27.2% on SWE-bench Verified - up to 540% over the base model and 256% over unfiltered fine-tuning." Per model on SWE-bench Verified: 3.2% -> 17.4% (Qwen3-8B), 4.6% -> 17.8% (Qwen3-14B), 9.0% -> 27.2% (Qwen3-32B) versus Original; 6.8% -> 17.4%, 9.4% -> 17.8%, 15.6% -> 27.2% versus FullData. SWE-bench Multilingual: "our approach improves over the Original baseline by 286% - 420%" (1.4% -> 4.0%, 4.3% -> 9.7%, 3.3% -> 14%). Metric-based filtering baseline: 14.4% vs 17.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 4.7% vs 6.7% on Multilingual (Qwen3-8B).
notes: Main methodological concern for a reviewer: the architectural-quality outcome is measured by AQJ, the same author-built LLM judge that was used to select the training data, so the headline NF improvement is partly circular; the judge is never validated against human expert ratings (only against static metrics, where it deliberately does not correlate), and the LLM backbone powering the judges is nowhere identified. Against the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural-conformance gain essentially disappears (83.6 vs 87.5, 87.1 vs 83.9, 93.5 vs 93.3), so the clear NF gain is only versus the untuned base model; the paper's distinctive claim versus FullData is about resolved rate and data efficiency, not conformance. Table 1 is hard to read because the AQJ columns are reported as relative changes to each model's own baseline while the baseline row is absolute, and the extraction garbles one cell ('17,1' for 17.1). Internal inconsistencies to check: the abstract says 286-424% cross-language improvement while Section 5.2 says 286-420%; Section 5.1 says 'improves the resolved rate by 174% - 256% compared to using the full dataset' where those figures are ratios rather than percentage improvements; Table 3's first row is labelled 'Original' with size 5,000 and value 6.8%, which is the FullData condition in Table 1, not the untuned base model; Table 3 lists SWE-Multi 5.0% for that row while Table 2 gives FullData Qwen3-8B as 3.0%. Tables 4 and 5 appear to have their captions swapped relative to their contents (the 'ACJ-style' table uses AQJ-correlated features). Results are single pass@1 runs with no variance, repeated runs or statistical tests, and no compute/cost figures despite the paper itself noting the token cost of agentic judging.
family_reason: The judges only filter a pool of existing trajectories; what changes the model's behaviour is supervised fine-tuning on the filtered set, so the training step does the work.
scope_reason: The reported non-functional outcome is the architectural conformance (structural quality) of the patches the fine-tuned models generate.
gain_metric: share of generated patches rated High or High-with-concerns by the Architecture Quality Judge, Qwen3-32B on SWE-bench Verified (%)
baseline_name: FullData (fine-tuned on the whole 5,000-trajectory pool); the untuned base model is the weaker baseline at 72.1
gain_quote:
Compared to FullData, our approach achieves comparable architectural quality — with High+HWC proportions of 83.6% vs.
87.5% on Qwen3-8B, 87.1% vs. 83.9% on Qwen314B, and 93.5% vs. 93.3% on Qwen3-32B
gain_note: Table 1 plus the RQ1 text. Against the untuned base model the same metric rises 60.9 -> 83.6 (8B), 64.0 -> 87.1 (14B) and 72.1 -> 93.5 (32B), which is the abstract's '61-72% to 84-94%', but against the strongest baseline (unfiltered fine-tuning) the architectural gain is a wash: 83.6 vs 87.5 on 8B, 87.1 vs 83.9 on 14B, 93.5 vs 93.3 on 32B. Table 1 prints the AQJ columns as deltas relative to each model's own baseline row, and one Acceptable cell is garbled ('17,1').
core_idea: Two agentic LLM judges, one scoring how much repository-specific architectural understanding a task needs and one scoring how well a patch respects conventions inferred from the repository itself, select which agent trajectories go into the supervised fine-tuning set.
core_idea_checked: Section 3: ACJ screens trivial patches, explores outward from changed files, rates five complexity axes; AQJ generates a repository- and issue-specific rubric with priority-ordered axes and prose anchors, then evaluates each axis in a separate sub-agent and synthesises a four-tier verdict; examples above both thresholds are kept and trained with loss masked to assistant tokens only.
note: The curation pipeline and the fine-tuned models are not tied to a domain, but the headline quality metric is repository-level and is produced by the same judge that selected the training data.

title: SecureVibe: Making Vibe Coding More Secure
technique_name: SecureVibe (Security Suite SFT + SecureVibe_rl GRPO / SecureVibe_hg hint-guided on-policy self-distillation)
metrics: security: SecPass pass@1 (solutions passing both functional and security tests/expert exploits) [execution]; per-CWE SecPass [execution]
benchmarks: PatchEval-Gen (200 tasks, 100 held-out validation), AutoBaxBench (560 tasks, 420 validation), BaxBench (392 tasks), SusVibes (186 tasks), unseen-CWE subsets (SusVibes 78, BaxBench 140), SWE-bench Verified (500)

baselines: Qwen 3.5 35B base; Security Only SFT; Simple Mixture SFT; Security Only SFT + GRPO; GPT 5.6 Sol and MiniMax M2.7 as reference
