effect_correctness_headline: it also improves functionality pass@1 by 13.6 points on the security coding task SusVibes and 4.1 points on the generic coding task SWE-bench Verified
notes: Only one model is trained (Qwen 3.5 35B); larger models are reference points only. Results are mean and std over 3 runs, with paired significance tests on the unseen-CWE subset. Overlap between PatchEval-Gen and SusVibes was removed and online git retrieval was blocked during SusVibes evaluation, but pretraining contamination is not discussed. Hardware (8 B200 GPUs) is reported but not training time, tokens or calls. No threats-to-validity section, only caveats in Appendix B. Table 1 is garbled in extraction.
family_reason: The contribution is a training recipe: supervised fine-tuning on a four-task security suite followed by reinforcement learning on execution rewards or hint-guided on-policy self-distillation; nothing changes at inference time.
scope_reason: The outcome is the security of code the agent writes, measured by security tests and expert exploits on repository-level tasks.
gain_metric: SecPass pass@1 on BaxBench (share of solutions passing both functional and security tests, %)
baseline_name: Qwen 3.5 35B base model (the same model without the recipe)
gain_quote:
Specifically, S ECURE V IBE improves
the security pass@1 by 6.9 points on BaxBench.
gain_note: Quote is the abstract's statement of the gain; the underlying numbers are Table 2 (BaxBench SecPass: base 19.71 +/- 1.15, SecureVibe_rl 26.62 +/- 1.88, mean over 3 runs). The other reference models in that table (GPT 5.6 Sol, MiniMax M2.7) are much larger models shown for context, not baselines for the recipe. Functional pass@1 also rises (32.91 -> 41.07 on BaxBench, and +4.1 points on SWE-bench Verified).
core_idea: Fine-tune a coding agent on a mixture of functionality coding, security-guided coding, security planning and security-test writing, then push it further with either reinforcement learning on functional-plus-security test outcomes or distillation from a copy of itself that was given the vulnerability hints.
core_idea_checked: Sections 3.2-3.3 and Appendix D/E: the Security Suite has 1,648 curated trajectories across the four tasks, the RL stage uses GRPO with a graded reward (1 for functional plus security, 0.5 functional only, negatives for unusable patches) and dynamic sampling, and the hint-guided stage uses on-policy self-distillation where the teacher sees level-4 hints the student never sees.
note: Only one model (Qwen 3.5 35B) is trained, results are means over three runs with paired significance tests on the unseen-CWE subsets, and the hint-guided variant trades some functional correctness for security on the training benchmarks.

title: LLM-Vectorizer: LLM-Based Verified Loop Vectorizer

models: GPT-4 (API 2023-08-01-preview), closed, general instruct

scope_reason: The outcome is the run-time efficiency of the vectorized C code the model produces, although the comparison is against compilers rather than against the model without the agent loop.
gain_metric: run-time speedup of the generated AVX2 code over auto-vectorizing compilers, across the 57 formally verified TSVC tests
baseline_name: state-of-the-art auto-vectorizing compilers GCC 10.5.0, Clang 19.0.0 and ICC 2021.10.0 (each normalised to 1.0)

found that LLMs are capable of producing high-performance
vectorized code with run-time speedup ranging from 1.1𝑥
to 9.4𝑥 as compared to the state-of-the-art compilers.

core_idea: A finite-state machine of GPT-4 agents rewrites scalar C loops into AVX2 intrinsics using Clang dependence analysis as input and checksum test feedback for repair, and the result is then checked for equivalence with the bounded translation validator Alive2.
core_idea_checked: Sections 2.2 and 3: the FSM runs vectorizer and compiler-tester agents for up to ten attempts with checksum testing as the plausibility criterion, then Alive2 with three domain-specific scaling tricks (loop alignment and unroll-factor matching, C-level unrolling, spatial case splitting) decides equivalence.
note: The task is rewriting existing C loops into AVX2 intrinsics on the TSVC compiler test suite, which cannot be run on function-level general benchmarks.

title: KernelSkill: A Multi-Agent Framework for GPU Kernel Optimization
technique_name: KernelSkill (multi-agent Generator/Reviewer/Planner/Optimizer/Diagnoser/Repairer loop with long-term expert-skill memory and short-term trajectory memory)
metrics: efficiency: average speedup vs Torch Eager, Fast1 (fraction at least as fast as Torch) [execution]; correctness: Success (compiles and matches PyTorch reference within tolerance) [execution]
benchmarks: KernelBench Levels 1-3 (100 + 100 + 50 = 250 tasks)
models: ChatGPT-5.1 (GPT-5.1), closed, general/reasoning
baselines: Kevin-32B, Astra, PRAGMA, CudaForge, QiMeng, STARK (STARK and QiMeng numbers taken from their papers; Astra and PRAGMA reimplemented); ablations w/o memory, w/o short-term memory, w/o long-term memory
effect_target_headline: average speedups of 5.44x, 2.82x, and 1.92x over Torch Eager on Levels 1, 2, and 3; vs STARK +79.5% on Level 1 (5.44 vs. 3.03), +4.8% on Level 2 (2.82 vs. 2.69), and +21.5% on Level 3 (1.92 vs. 1.58)
effect_correctness_headline: 100% success rate on KernelBench Levels 1-3 (w/o memory: 0.96, 0.98, 0.94)
notes: Only one LLM (GPT-5.1) used. Baseline numbers for STARK and QiMeng copied from original papers (different hardware/setup possible), Astra/PRAGMA reimplemented; comparability caveat. STARK has higher Fast1 on Levels 1 and 3 (0.71 vs 0.62; 0.87 vs 0.82). Compute reported only as refinement rounds (15 vs STARK 30), no tokens/cost. Tables extracted as flattened columns but values reconstructable. No threats-to-validity section; brief limitation in conclusion.
family_reason: The system is a closed loop of specialised agents (Generator, Reviewer with compiler/verifier/profiler, Feature Extractor, Planner, Optimizer, Diagnoser, Repairer); the knowledge memory feeds the Planner but the agent loop carries the optimization.
scope_reason: The outcome is the execution speed of the GPU kernels the LLM writes, with correctness held at 100%.

gain_quote:
Compared with the strongest baseline in speedup (STARK), KernelSkill improves average speedup by +79.5% on Level 1
(5.44 vs. 3.03, +2.41× absolute)
gain_note: Table 1 and Section 5.4. STARK's and QiMeng's numbers are copied from their own papers (possibly different hardware), Astra and PRAGMA were reimplemented by these authors, so comparability is imperfect. STARK still has a higher Fast1 on Levels 1 and 3 (0.71 vs 0.62 and 0.87 vs 0.82), i.e. KernelSkill's mean speedup advantage is not matched by a higher share of kernels that beat PyTorch.
core_idea: A multi-agent generate-profile-plan-repair loop for CUDA kernels that picks its optimization moves from a curated long-term store of expert optimization rules matched by deterministic rules over profiler and code features, and keeps a short-term per-task trajectory so it does not retry what already failed.
core_idea_checked: Sections 4.1-4.2 and Algorithm 1: three seed kernels per task, up to 15 refinement rounds, a two-branch loop (repair when compilation or correctness fails, otherwise optimize), long-term memory curated from a GPU optimization survey into a deterministic decision policy plus method knowledge, and short-term repair and optimization trajectories injected into later prompts.
note: Only one backbone model (GPT-5.1) and CUDA kernels on KernelBench, so it cannot be run on function-level general benchmarks.

scope_reason: The outcome is the execution speed of HGEMM CUDA kernels written by the trained model.

title: EvoVerilog: Large Langugage Model Assisted Evolution of Verilog Code

title: K-Search: LLM Kernel Generation via Co-Evolving Intrinsic World Model

title: KernelArc: A Multi-Agent Framework for GPU Kernel Optimization

title: RTLScout: Joint Agentic Code and Synthesis Optimization for Efficient Digital Circuits
technique_name: RTLScout: four-phase pipeline combining ReAct agentic RTL rewriting, agent-guided synthesis optimization via source-local @abc_optimized decorators, arithmetic-architecture selection (sweep or @arithmetic_optimized decorator), and high-effort gate-level Deepsyn refinement, run inside a multi-run elite pool with z-score softmax seeding and lessons-learned feedback; Spire, a Python-embedded HDL, is introduced to carry source-local optimization intent
metrics: efficiency: post-mapping circuit area (um^2), delay (ps), area-delay product (10^3 um^2.ps), power, and Yosys post-synth cell count and CMOS transistor estimate [all tool-static / execution via Yosys + OpenROAD STA on ASAP7]; correctness: simulation pass rate against a golden self-checking testbench (exhaustive over all 2^32 input pairs for fpmul_f16; 16M/2M/>=10k vectors for the larger designs and RTLRewriter cases), Verilator lint, plus post-hoc combinational/sequential equivalence checking [execution]
benchmarks: fpmul_f16 (IEEE-754-compliant FP16 multiplier with subnormals, primary benchmark); fpadd_f32 (IEEE-754 binary32 adder); PDPU-16 posit dot-product unit, combinational and 5-stage pipelined tops; the 14 short-bench control-and-datapath cases of the RTLRewriter benchmark
models: GLM 5.2 (open-weights) as the underlying LLM for the agent campaigns
baselines: Starting (unoptimized) design; Deepsyn-only at matched compute (700x20 min and 700x40 min); phase-ablated configurations (Phase 3 only, Phases 1+2, Phases 1+3, Phases 1-3); commercial Cadence Genus reference FP16 multiplier from Larsson-Edefors on the same ASAP7 PDK; published RTLRewriter reference designs; an otherwise identical Verilog pipeline (for the Spire-vs-Verilog comparison)
effect_target_headline: On an IEEE-754-compliant 16-bit floating-point multiplier with subnormal support, RTLScout reduces area by 34% and delay by 38% relative to a starting design and outperforms a commercial-tool reference design on the ASAP7 technology. On 14 RTLRewriter benchmarks, the Spire-based pipeline achieves 16.3% lower mean per-case Yosys cell count than an otherwise identical Verilog pipeline. (fpmul_f16 best area 116 -> 77 um^2, best delay 1530 -> 949 ps; RTLRewriter mean per-case cell-count reduction vs the RTLRewriter reference: 10.9% Verilog, 25.8% Spire)
effect_correctness_headline: A best-design tracker snapshots every evaluation that achieves 100% correctness at lower cost; every Pareto-optimal fpmul_f16 design reported in this paper is furthermore verified exhaustively: all 2^32 input pairs are simulated at the gate level against a bit-exact golden model
notes: Domain is hardware RTL rather than general-purpose software; the NF dimension is circuit efficiency (area, delay, power, cell/transistor count) rather than program runtime, so a reviewer should confirm this fits the review's efficiency definition. Only one LLM (GLM 5.2) is evaluated, with no justification and no cross-model comparison. No threats-to-validity section and no contamination discussion, although the RTLRewriter benchmark is public. Tables 1, 4 and 5 are badly garbled in PDF extraction (column values run together); headline numbers were taken from the abstract, Section 5.3, Section 7 and the conclusion rather than from the garbled table cells. Cost reported precisely in Table 2 ($65.07 total for fpmul_f16, $0.04 per core-hour); context window growth reported as ~36k to ~69k tokens per run.
family_reason: A ReAct agent repeatedly writes RTL and calls an evaluation tool that returns lint, simulation pass rate and post-mapping area/delay/power, and the best-design tracker plus multi-run elite pool simply ratchet on that measured feedback.
scope_reason: The outcome is the physical efficiency (area, delay, cell and transistor count) of LLM-written hardware source, with functional correctness verified separately.
gain_metric: mean per-case reduction in Yosys post-synthesis cell count on the 14 RTLRewriter short-bench cases (percent reduction)
baseline_name: RTLRewriter published reference implementations (prior cost-aware MCTS RTL rewriter)
gain_quote:
Both pipelines outperform the RTLRewriter reference designs (Table 4), achieving mean per-case
reductions in Yosys cell count of 10.9% for Verilog and 25.8% for Spire
gain_note: Section 7.2 and Table 4; baseline_value 0 means the RTLRewriter reference is the zero point of the reduction. Means are over per-repetition bests, n=3. The main study is a different metric: on fpmul_f16 the full pipeline reaches 77 um2 best area and 949 ps best delay versus 116 um2 / 1530 ps for the starting design and 89 um2 / 1000 ps for the matched-compute Deepsyn-only baseline (Table 1), and the Phase 4 front beats a Cadence Genus commercial reference.
core_idea: An LLM agent rewrites RTL in Spire, a Python-embedded HDL where optimisation intent is expressed as source-local decorators, inside a multi-run elite pool with lessons-learned seeding, followed by arithmetic-architecture selection and high-effort gate-level Deepsyn refinement.
core_idea_checked: Verified in Section 3: ReAct loop with file and run_evaluation tools, @abc_optimized and @arithmetic_optimized decorators compiled through ABC and a verified arithmetic library, z-score softmax elite-pool seeding, and a four-phase pipeline whose ablation (Table 1, Fig. 4a) shows no single phase reaches the full-pipeline front.
note: Hardware RTL with circuit area and delay as the efficiency dimension, so it cannot run on software function-level benchmarks.

title: FABRICA: Agentic CUDA-to-CSL Translation and Optimization for Wafer-Scale Systems
technique_name: FABRICA: six-stage role-specialized agentic workflow (analyst, architect, implementer, reviewer, optimizer plus reference-isolation firewall) with retrieval from a consolidated Cerebras knowledge base, starter templates, failure-classified execution repair, and correctness-gated cycle optimization (an edit is accepted only if it stays valid and reduces median device cycles)
metrics: efficiency: in-kernel device cycle count and geometric-mean speedup over the same-target expert CSL reference, measured on the SDK fabric simulator and on WSE-3 hardware [execution]; correctness: bundle pass rate (compile + run + host/device contract preservation + valid timing path + numerical agreement on visible and held-out inputs), with six integrity checks against reference leakage and disabled timers [execution]
benchmarks: FABRICA-BENCH, introduced here: 49 paired CUDA/CSL tasks across four construction levels; a frozen 28-task Level 1-3 core set; an 8-task diagnostic set (5 runs each); a 15-task knowledge panel; a 12-task cross-model probe; 14 references for the optimization-only study; 35 bundles in the hardware-replay set (27 timing-comparable pairs)
models: Claude Opus 4.8 (closed, primary); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed); Claude Opus 4.6 (closed); gpt-oss-120b (open-weight); Gemma 4 31B (open-weight); gpt-oss-20b (open-weight); five further open-weight models on the probe; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B used in the LoRA SFT pilot
baselines: Single-attempt generation with retrieval, review, repair and optimization disabled; expert-written CSL reference implementations in the benchmark bundles; ablation modes A (unguided), B (+classified execution repair), C (A + design records), D (B + design records), T (B + starting template); knowledge tiers (full knowledge / no retrieved Cerebras material / also no CSL primer)
effect_target_headline: For 27 generated/reference pairs with device-internal timing, geometric-mean speedup is 3.75x on the SDK simulator and 3.47x on WSE-3 hardware; by level on WSE-3: Level 1 7.49x, Level 2 2.56x, Level 3 2.71x, Level 4 1.24x; the optimization-only study improves all 14 measured references with a 1.44x geometric-mean speedup and seven programs improving by at least 25%
effect_correctness_headline: On a fixed 28-task Level 1-3 core comparison with Claude Opus 4.8, FABRICA raises success from 6/28 to 26/28; across the 49-task coverage evaluation, 38 tasks produce a correct program; the final three tasks are evaluated over three seeds and pass 8/9 runs; retrieved Cerebras knowledge separately raises success from 1/15 to 7/15
notes: Contamination and leakage are handled unusually carefully: a reference-isolation firewall, held-out inputs and seeds, six integrity checks, disjoint train/test splits, GEMM and GEMV held train-only because retrieved WaferLLM patterns overlap those families, and benchmark-disjoint filtering for the SFT pilot. The paper also contains a secondary training-time contribution (LoRA SFT on 6,066 harvested CUDA-to-CSL records for Qwen3-8B/14B) but reports only SDK-free structural proxy metrics (usable/contract/chrF/CSL vocabulary), not executable correctness or efficiency, so it is not recorded as a separate technique. 'Full prompts, candidates, checks, and measurements remain in the artifact' but no artifact URL is printed in the text. Attempt budgets are reported per study; no token, dollar or wall-clock cost is given. Figures 5-8 and several tables are garbled in PDF extraction (axis labels split per character); headline numbers were taken from the abstract, Section V and the conclusion.
family_reason: The role-specialised stages form the harness, but the only single-variable ablation that moves results strongly is retrieved Cerebras knowledge (1/15 to 7/15 with model, reviewer and attempt budget fixed), whereas the design-record and template variations leave success essentially unchanged.
scope_reason: The outcome is the device-cycle efficiency (and correctness) of LLM-generated CSL kernel code translated from CUDA and then optimised.
gain_metric: geometric-mean speedup of the generated CSL program over the same-target expert CSL reference, 27 timing-comparable pairs
baseline_name: expert-written CSL reference implementation in the benchmark bundle
gain_quote: All 27: geomean 3.75x simulator / 3.47x WSE-3
gain_note: Figure 6 caption text; the same numbers appear in the abstract and conclusion (3.75x on the SDK simulator, 3.47x on WSE-3 hardware). The reference is the comparison point, so its speedup is 1 by construction. A cleaner optimisation-only measurement (W2, starting from correct CSL) gives a 1.44x geometric mean over 14 references. The correctness co-outcome is 6/28 to 26/28 on the fixed Level 1-3 core with Claude Opus 4.8.
core_idea: A six-stage role-specialised agentic workflow (analyst, architect, implementer, reviewer, optimiser behind a reference-isolation firewall) translates CUDA to Cerebras CSL using retrieval from a consolidated SDK knowledge base, classified execution-failure repair, and cycle optimisation gated on held-out correctness.
core_idea_checked: Verified in Section III: firewall, deterministic extractor and record parser, role-filtered retrieval with leave-one-out worked examples, compile-only gate then staged repair routing, and an optimiser that accepts an edit only when it stays valid and lowers median device cycles (Eq. 2).
note: Wafer-scale accelerator kernel translation (CUDA to CSL); the paper also contributes FABRICA-BENCH, but the framework itself is a reusable method.

title: AscendCraft: Automatic Ascend NPU Kernel Generation via DSL-Guided Transcompilation
technique_name: AscendCraft (DSL-guided generation + multi-pass LLM transcompilation with per-pass compiler-error feedback)
metrics: efficiency: Fast0.2@1 / Fast0.8@1 / Fast1.0@1, percentage of correct kernels whose execution time is within x× of PyTorch eager reference, measured by on-device kernel execution [execution]; speedup over PyTorch eager for mHC case study [execution]. No threats-to-validity section, no ablation, no artifact link, no repeated runs or variance, no cost/token reporting, and no contamination discussion. Efficiency here is kernel runtime performance; no readability or security measurement. family_reason: The mechanism is constrained staged prompting: generate in a purpose-built DSL from hand-written category-specific exemplars, then lower it through four structured single-concern prompts, with compiler errors used only as a per-pass repair signal.
scope_reason: The outcome is the correctness and execution efficiency of LLM-generated AscendC NPU kernel code relative to PyTorch eager execution.
gain_metric: Fast1.0@1, percentage of generated kernels whose execution time matches or exceeds PyTorch eager (52 MultiKernelBench Ascend kernels)
baseline_name: PyTorch eager execution on Ascend (the performance reference)
gain_quote:
82.7% of kernels achieve at least 20% of PyTorch
eager performance, 57.7% reach 80%, and 46.2% match or
exceed the eager baseline.
gain_note: Section 5.3 and Table 2; Fast0.2 82.7, Fast0.8 57.7, Fast1.0 46.2. baseline_value is left empty because Fast_x is defined relative to PyTorch eager (the reference is 100% by construction) and no prior method reports Fast_x on this benchmark; the only prior-method number is correctness, 13.0% for Claude Sonnet-4 reported in MultiKernelBench versus 90.4% Pass@1 here. core_idea: Ascend NPU kernels are first generated in a lightweight Ascend-aware DSL from category-specific expert examples, then transcompiled into AscendC through four constrained LLM lowering passes with per-pass compiler-error correction.

note: AscendC NPU kernels only; the approach depends on hand-written per-category DSL exemplars and cannot run on general-purpose function-level benchmarks.

title: GenDB: The Next Generation of Query Processing - Synthesized, Not Engineered
technique_name: GenDB (multi-agent LLM pipeline: Workload Analyzer, Storage/Index Designer, Query Planner, Code Generator, Query Optimizer, with iterative runtime-feedback refinement)
metrics: efficiency: per-query and total hot-run execution time in ms, and speedup factors versus baseline engines [execution]; generation cost in US dollars and generation time in minutes [execution/reported]. Correctness: validated by comparing generated query results against a traditional DBMS (e.g., DuckDB) ground truth, reported qualitatively only [execution]
benchmarks: TPC-H scale factor 10, representative subset Q1, Q3, Q6, Q9, Q18 (5 queries); SEC-EDGAR, a new manually constructed benchmark from SEC financial statement data 2022-2024 (5 GB), 1,000 SQLSmith-generated queries diversity-sampled down to six queries
models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, closed, instruct/reasoning; selected to balance cost and performance
baselines: State-of-the-art query engines DuckDB, Umbra, MonetDB, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL (with default indexes, and with GenDB-generated additional indexes); ablation baselines: Single-Agent (Guided) and Single-Agent (High-Level)
effect_target_headline: On TPC-H, GenDB achieves a total execution time of 214 ms across five representative queries. This result is 2.8x faster than DuckDB (594 ms) and Umbra (590 ms), which are the two fastest baselines, and 11.2x faster than ClickHouse. On SEC-EDGAR, GenDB achieves 328 ms, which is 5.0x faster than DuckDB and 3.9x faster than Umbra. Ablation: multi-agent 236 ms on TPC-H, 1.2x faster than the best single-agent variant (guided, 281 ms); on SEC-EDGAR the gap widens to 2.3x over guided (752 ms) and 4.1x over high-level (1,325 ms)

Correctness is validated against a reference DBMS but no quantitative correctness rate (e.g., pass rate) is reported anywhere, so QA4 is partial. Only one LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6) is used, justified briefly on cost/performance grounds. No repeated runs, variance or statistical tests. Contamination is explicitly addressed by constructing the SEC-EDGAR benchmark to reduce TPC-H leakage from LLM training data. Limitations are discussed at length in the research-agenda section but there is no formal threats-to-validity section. Efficiency here is query execution runtime of the LLM-generated C++ code; no readability or security measurement.
family_reason: The system is a pipeline of five dedicated LLM agents (workload analyser, storage/index designer, query planner, code generator, query optimiser), and the ablation attributes the gain to that decomposition over guided and high-level single agents.
scope_reason: The outcome is the runtime efficiency of LLM-generated C++ query execution code, validated for correctness against a traditional DBMS.
gain_metric: total hot-run execution time in ms across five representative TPC-H SF=10 queries
baseline_name: DuckDB v1.4.4 (fastest baseline engine, tied with Umbra)
gain_quote:
This result is 2.8× faster than DuckDB (594 ms) and
Umbra (590 ms), which are the two fastest baselines
gain_note: Section 4.2; GenDB total 214 ms versus DuckDB 594 ms and Umbra 590 ms on TPC-H Q1/Q3/Q6/Q9/Q18, and 328 ms versus 5.0x slower DuckDB on SEC-EDGAR. The ablation against single-agent variants (236 ms multi-agent vs 281 ms guided vs 456 ms high-level on TPC-H) uses slightly different totals than the main figure. core_idea: Instead of a fixed query engine, a pipeline of LLM agents analyses the workload and hardware, designs storage and indexes, plans the query, generates per-query C++ executables, and iteratively refines them from runtime feedback.

title: Securing LLM-Generated Embedded Firmware Through AI Agent-Driven Validation and Patching
technique_name: Three-phase LLM firmware generation with multi-agent validation and iterative CWE-guided patching (Threat Detection Agent, Performance Optimization Agent, Compliance Verification Agent)
metrics: security: Vulnerability Remediation Rate VRR = fixed/identified vulnerabilities x 100 [tool-static + execution]; Security Coverage Index SCI, a weighted combination of fuzzing, static-analysis and dynamic-analysis coverage [tool-static + execution]; Threat Model Compliance Score TMCS = mitigated/identified threats x 100 [tool-static]; Agent Detection Accuracy ADA = (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN) versus ground truth [tool-static]. efficiency: Worst-Case Execution Time WCET in ms and Task Jitter in microseconds, measured in the virtualized RTOS [execution]; deadline misses logged. Pipeline: Iteration Efficiency Index IEI
benchmarks: No standard benchmark; custom firmware components built by the authors (SensorTask, NetworkTask, MQTT message handling with minimal detection and parsing) on FreeRTOS under QEMU; the number of tasks or firmware programs is never stated
models: GPT-4, closed, instruct (OpenAI); GPT-3.5, Code Llama and PaLM 2 mentioned only as related work; the AI agents are said to be powered by unnamed specialized machine-learning models trained on domain-specific datasets

(9) Research questions RQ1-RQ3 in Section II are not directly answered by the results section; the paper reads partly as a methodology/experimental-plan paper.

title: FlashVector: Agent for Hierarchical Model Serving Stack Optimization
technique_name: FlashVector (layer-agent abstraction with a knowledge base and a Profile-Diagnose-Optimize-Verify loop plus a post-run Refine stage; optimize locally, verify globally; always-on self-retriggering loop)
metrics: efficiency: latency speedup and throughput increase versus the production baseline; sustained requests per second per pod at a fixed latency SLO; p99 latency in ms; per-kernel latency in microseconds; percentage of GPU time and dispatcher overhead; per-call-site kernel speedup factors [all execution]. Correctness: element-wise output comparison against recorded baseline predictions, with class-dependent bars (bit-exact for deterministic rewrites; 1e-3 element-wise absolute deviation with at most 0.1% of elements beyond it for floating-point reordering, 1e-4 for FP32 serving; business metrics for intentional approximations; shadow-traffic canary for configuration changes) [execution]
benchmarks: No public benchmark; evaluated in situ on Unity's Vector advertising platform. Table 1 reports 6 production models (Retrieval model, Ranking models 1-4, Gamer model); Table 3 reports one preprocessor service across 3 cumulative optimization stages; Table 4 reports 4 production models (A-D) for configuration tuning; Table 2 reports 5 Cython kernel replacements
models: Not reported anywhere in the paper; the underlying LLM powering the agents is never named
baselines: Existing hand-tuned production stack: for Case 2 an AOT-compiled (PyTorch AOTInductor), FP16-quantized model on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with batch size 2000; for Case 3 a 940 RPS/pod preprocessor baseline; for Case 4 a hand-tuned configuration left at the framework default batch size with utilization-target scaling
effect_target_headline: FlashVector achieved up to 2x throughput increase and up to 1.98x latency speedup on model server, and up to 1.6x throughput increase on feature store. Case 1: speed up to 30x on the Triton input-conversion step. Case 2: attention latency cut from 996.5 microseconds to 279.8 microseconds (a 3.56x speedup); embedding changes reduce total GPU kernel time by 33.4%, cut forward-pass latency by 30.1%, and lower dispatcher overhead from 44.8% to 28.5%. Case 3: 940 requests per second at baseline, roughly 1.5k with all three in place, a 1.6x improvement
effect_correctness_headline: Because the fused kernel preserves the original operation order and accumulation precision, it generates attention weights that are bit-identical to the baseline, which we verify by element-wise comparison
notes: ELIGIBILITY IS BORDERLINE and a human reviewer should confirm the call. The system optimizes an existing, human-written production codebase (NVIDIA Triton C++, a Python feature-processing service, PyTorch model code) rather than generating programs from a specification, which looks like the 'adjacent' side list (LLM refactoring of human-written code / EC4). It was included because IC2 explicitly admits code 'edited by an LLM', EC4 requires 'no LLM generation', and the agent does write new code (a fused CUDA kernel, hand-written Cython kernels, a C++ rewrite of a deserialization path). Flip to exclude/EC4/adjacent if the review intends EC4 to cover LLM-driven optimization of existing code. Other issues: (1) The underlying LLM is NEVER named anywhere in the paper, so QA5 is 0 and reimplementation is not possible. (2) This is an industrial experience report of case studies, not a controlled evaluation: there is no ablation, no public benchmark, no artifact release, and no threats-to-validity section. (3) The agent's correctness verification is well specified (bit-exactness and tolerance bars per change class) but no aggregate correctness results are reported. (4) Measurement noise is handled rigorously (noise floor estimated from repeated no-op baseline runs, re-measurement at larger sample sizes), which is the strongest methodological element. (5) Tables 1-4 are garbled by PDF extraction: Table 1's column values are split from the model names, Table 2's left column (Python functions replaced) is separated from its speedup column, and Table 4's header row is interleaved; the mappings are recoverable but should be re-checked against the original. (6) Figures 2-6 are referenced but their content is not in the extracted text. (7) Section 5.2 text appears out of order in the extraction (Case 3 baseline setup text is interleaved into Case 2). (8) The only URL given is a GitHub issue for a contributed upstream fix (https://github.com/triton-inference-server/server/issues/8348), not a research artifact.
family_reason: A profile-diagnose-optimize-verify loop driven by profiler measurements and a noise-floor acceptance gate does the work; the knowledge base is supporting context.
scope_reason: Optimizes an existing human-written production serving stack (Triton C++, Python preprocessor, PyTorch model, GPU kernels) rather than LLM-generated programs from a specification; the LLM-edited code's efficiency is the outcome.
gain_quote: the attention latency from 996.5 µs to 279.8 µs (a 3.56× speedup).
gain_note: Headline in abstract is up to 2x throughput and 1.98x latency (Table 1, six production models) but no single quoted span holds both numbers for those; the quoted case is one fused-attention kernel. Table 3: preprocessor 940 to about 1.5k RPS/pod. All results are in-house case studies; the LLM is never named.
core_idea: An always-on agent loop that profiles one serving-stack layer at a time, diagnoses bottlenecks against a layer knowledge base, applies a code or configuration change, and accepts it only if a full-stack load test shows gains above measurement noise.
core_idea_checked: Layer-agent abstraction (Profile, Diagnose, Optimize, Verify, plus post-run Refine of the knowledge base) applied to GPU kernels, computation graph, model server and feature processing; optimize locally, verify globally with replayed production traffic.
note: Industrial case-study paper on Unity's production serving stack; no public benchmark, no named LLM, no code.

title: ConCuR: Conciseness Makes State-of-the-Art Kernel Generation
technique_name: ConCuR data synthesis and conciseness-based curation plus LoRA supervised fine-tuning (yielding KernelCoder)
metrics: efficiency: speedup = T_Torch / T_kernel times the correctness indicator, measured by execution against torch eager; fast1 = fraction of tasks with speedup greater than 1; Gspeedup = geometric average of speedups [all execution]. Correctness: Exec, the execution correct rate, where generated kernel output must match the PyTorch reference in dimension and value on random input [execution]. Auxiliary: ARL, average reasoning length in tokens, proposed as a task-difficulty indicator
benchmarks: KernelBench Levels 1 and 2 (200 tasks total; the difficulty division in Table 4 sums to 37 easy + 114 medium + 49 hard = 200). Levels 3 and 4 were excluded as beyond current model capability. Training data: ConCuR, 4,892 curated examples drawn from 90,810 synthesized (PyTorch, CUDA kernel, CoT) triples over 18,162 KernelBook tasks, of which 9,789 tasks had at least one correct generation and 24,136 kernels were correct
models: KernelCoder, 32B, open, reasoning (LoRA fine-tune of QwQ-32B); data synthesized by Kevin-32B, 32B, open, reasoning. Baselines evaluated: DeepSeek-R1-0528 685B open reasoning (Triton and CUDA); DeepSeek-V3.1-Think 685B open reasoning; Qwen3-Coder-Plus 480B code-specialized; GPT-4o closed; Claude-4-Sonnet closed; QwQ-32B open reasoning; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B open; Llama-3.3-70B open; AutoTriton 8B open fine-tuned; KernelLLM 8B open fine-tuned; Kevin 32B open RL-trained; AI CUDA Engineer with o1-preview and o1-high (pass@10 table only)
baselines: Base model QwQ-32B; frontier models (DeepSeek-R1-0528, DeepSeek-V3.1-Think, Qwen3-Coder-Plus, GPT-4o, Claude-4-Sonnet); prior fine-tuned kernel models (Kevin, KernelLLM, AutoTriton); and four data-curation ablations trained with identical settings: 5K-random, 5K-max (the s1 longest-reasoning method), 5K-min, 5K-speedup; plus a dataset-size ablation at 552 / 1105 / 2210 / 4892 samples
effect_target_headline: Pass@1 fast1 on KernelBench: KernelCoder (32B) 17.0 on Level 1 and 39.0 on Level 2, versus its base model QwQ-32B at 7.0 and 11.0, versus Kevin (32B) at 16.0 and 27.0, and versus DeepSeek-R1-0528 (CUDA, 685B) at 18.0 and 38.0. Pass@10 fast1: KernelCoder 32.0 (Level 1) and 68.0 (Level 2) versus QwQ-32B 12.0 and 46.0. Ablation (Table 3, pass@1 / pass@10 fast1): KernelCoder 17.0 / 32.0 on Level 1 and 39.0 / 68.0 on Level 2, versus 5K-random 9.0 / 21.0 and 24.0 / 55.0, 5K-max 7.0 / 17.0 and 27.0 / 50.0, 5K-min 10.0 / 23.0 and 26.0 / 55.0, 5K-speedup 8.0 / 21.0 and 21.0 / 56.0. However, on the difficulty split (Table 5, Gspeedup pass@10) KernelCoder reaches 1.319 / 0.831 / 0.410 on easy / medium / hard, below Qwen3-Coder-Plus at 1.468 / 1.152 / 0.741
effect_correctness_headline: Pass@1 Exec: KernelCoder 58.0 on Level 1 and 59.0 on Level 2, versus QwQ-32B 18.0 and 17.0, Kevin 50.0 and 46.0, DeepSeek-R1-0528 (CUDA) 52.0 and 55.0. Pass@10 Exec: KernelCoder 91.0 and 95.0, versus QwQ-32B 55.0 and 76.0, Kevin 86.0 and 90.0. Difficulty split Exec pass@10: KernelCoder 100.0 easy, 94.7 medium, 83.7 hard, the best of the five models compared
notes: Methodologically one of the stronger papers in this batch: detailed hyperparameters, the full inference prompt in Appendix C, four data-curation ablations trained under identical settings, a dataset-size ablation, a training-cost comparison table, and a reported Pearson correlation (r = -0.047, p < 0.01) for the speedup/reasoning-length relationship. Caveats for a human reviewer. (1) Tables 1 and 2 are badly garbled by PDF extraction: the model rows are separated from their numeric columns and in the Smaller-Scale block the fast1 columns carry only 7 values for 8 model rows, most plausibly because KernelLLM has no fast1 entry. The KernelCoder values quoted above were cross-validated against the ablation Table 3, which independently lists KernelCoder as 58.0 / 91.0 Exec and 17.0 / 32.0 fast1 on Level 1 and 59.0 / 95.0 Exec and 39.0 / 68.0 fast1 on Level 2, so the KernelCoder and base-model figures are reliable; other baselines' fast1 values should be re-checked against the original PDF. (2) Baselines are run in different target languages (some Triton, some CUDA), which the tables note but the comparison does not control for. (3) The headline 'state-of-the-art' claim rests on Exec and fast1; on the harder difficulty split the geometric mean speedup of KernelCoder is below Qwen3-Coder-Plus, and the paper's own Future Work concedes that generated kernels 'do not exhibit satisfactory performance (at least, better than Torch Eager)' across all models. (4) No threats-to-validity or limitations section. (5) Contamination is not discussed at all, despite training data (KernelBook PyTorch programs) and the evaluation benchmark (KernelBench) being drawn from closely related PyTorch program distributions. (6) The ConCuR dataset itself does not appear to have a release URL; only the KernelCoder model is linked. (7) Figures 2, 3 and 4 are rendered as scattered axis numbers in the extraction, so the distributional claims behind Observation 1 could not be verified from the text alone.
family_reason: Gains come from LoRA SFT of QwQ-32B on a curated dataset selected for short reasoning traces and high speedup.
scope_reason: Outcome is the speed (fast1 / speedup) of LLM-generated CUDA kernels.
gain_quote: in correctness (Exec) and performance (fast1 ) compared to our base model, QwQ-32B.
gain_note: Numbers from Table 1 (garbled extraction; values reconstructed by column order): KernelCoder L2 fast1 39.0 vs DeepSeek-R1-0528 CUDA 38.0 and base QwQ-32B 11.0. On Level 1 the strongest baseline DeepSeek-R1-0528 CUDA (18.0) slightly beats KernelCoder (17.0). The quoted sentence states the gain only against the base model; no sentence gives both numbers.
core_idea: Synthesize CUDA kernels with reasoning traces via Kevin-32B, keep correct ones where the shortest trace also has the top speedup (plus very fast kernels and a balanced single-operator share), and LoRA-fine-tune QwQ-32B on the 4,892 examples.
core_idea_checked: ConCuR: 90,810 Kevin-32B generations on KernelBook tasks, curated by conciseness-plus-speedup, single-operator balancing and speedup>5 kernels; LoRA SFT of QwQ-32B gives KernelCoder.
note: Only model weights are released (Hugging Face); efficiency gain over the strongest frontier baseline is marginal and reversed on Level 1.

title: Groupwise Agentic Grading and Advantage Redistribution for Code Agent RL
technique_name: Gagar (Groupwise Agentic Grading for Advantage Redistribution): an SFT-trained agentic grader ranks test-passing rollouts in a shared workspace on five code-quality criteria, and the resulting quality factors drive sum-preserving rescaling of positive advantages in GRPO-style code-agent RL
metrics: readability-maintainability: rubric-weighted quality score W = 0.30*approach suitability + 0.25*implementation precision + 0.20*minimality of changes + 0.15*unintended side effects + 0.10*codebase consistency, each scored 1 to 5 [llm-judge]; average win rate among test-passing candidates from joint groupwise rankings [llm-judge]; share of groups ranked first with ties split equally [llm-judge]; fraction of candidates in the highest quality tier T1 [llm-judge]. Correctness: avg@3 pass rate on DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro [execution]. Agent process cost (not code efficiency): mean main-agent interaction turns and mean total token length [execution]. Training diagnostics: policy entropy, policy-gradient loss, mean training-rollout length
benchmarks: DeepSWE v1.1 (long-horizon software development) and SWE-bench Pro (repository-level issue resolution); avg@3 with three samples per task. The implementation-quality evaluation uses a fixed random sample of 30 DeepSWE tasks, pooling up to three rollouts per method per task with anonymized identifiers and randomized order. Task counts for the full benchmarks are not stated
models: Policy models: MiMo-V2.6-Flash, 310B total / 15B active parameters, mixture-of-experts, proprietary (Xiaomi), initialized from a pre-RL SFT checkpoint; MiMo-V2.6-Pro, 1.02T total / 42B active parameters, mixture-of-experts, proprietary, likewise from a pre-RL SFT checkpoint. Online grader: the pre-RL SFT checkpoint of MiMo-V2.6-Pro (initially Claude Opus 5). Offline quality judge: Claude Opus 5, closed. External comparison models: Kimi K3 (2.8T), GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5
baselines: Binary-outcome reward RL without online quality grading, trained under identical settings and compared at shared steps; a downweighting-only ablation that applies quality factors without restoring removed positive credit or re-centering; external frontier models K3, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 for the mixed-task runs
effect_target_headline: At the final shared checkpoint, Gagar achieves a mean quality score of 4.03 versus 3.70 for the baseline, with an average win rate of 69.8% among passing candidates. It ranks first in 65.0% of groups after splitting ties. Across the audited checkpoints, improvements are most apparent in implementation precision, minimality of changes, and avoidance of unintended side effects; the fraction of candidates assigned to the highest-quality tier, T1, increases from 25.4% to 34.3%
effect_correctness_headline: At step 28, Gagar achieves 62.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, exceeding the baseline by 12.1 percentage points (the baseline fell from 58.5% at step 20 to 50.2%). With continued training, Gagar reaches a peak DeepSWE pass rate of 63.4% at step 44. On SWE-bench Pro, the baseline plateaus at approximately 59% from step 16 through step 28, whereas Gagar reaches 62.5% at step 52. After mixed-task RL, DeepSWE v1.1 avg@3 reaches 67.9 (Flash) and 71.9 (Pro), with SWE-bench Pro at 60.9 and 62.7
notes: Scope note for the reviewer: the five graded criteria (approach suitability, implementation precision, minimality of changes, unintended side effects, codebase consistency) map to the readability-maintainability dimension, and the paper frames them as producing 'maintainable, merge-ready code' that reduces developer review effort. The reported turn-count and token-length reductions (e.g. DeepSWE mean turns 132.3 to 111.6 and mean tokens 191.9k to 172.9k at step 28) are the AGENT'S process cost, not the runtime efficiency of the generated code, so they are recorded under compute_reported rather than as an efficiency outcome; a reviewer who treats agent cost as efficiency would add that dimension. Other caveats: (1) The quality evaluation is an LLM judge (Claude Opus 5) on only 30 DeepSWE tasks with up to three rollouts per method; it is blinded (anonymized identifiers, randomized order) but there is no human validation, no inter-rater agreement, and no check against the judge's own self-preference, even though Claude Opus 5 is simultaneously an external comparison model in Table 1 and was the original online grader. (2) No limitations or threats-to-validity section, no contamination discussion, no artifact release. (3) Single training run per condition and no confidence intervals or significance tests; the comparison is complicated by the baseline being stopped early at step 28 because of degradation. (4) The models (MiMo-V2.6-Flash and Pro), the grader checkpoint and the SFT data for the grader are all proprietary and undescribed, so the grading component cannot be reproduced; the advantage-redistribution mathematics and all its constants are fully specified in Section 3.3 and Appendix A. (5) Figures 2, 3 and 4 are reduced to scattered axis numbers by PDF extraction, so all numbers above were taken from the running text, which states them explicitly; Tables 1 and 2 extracted cleanly. (6) The programming language of the benchmarks is never stated.
family_reason: Gains come from RL training where an agentic grader's quality ranks redistribute GRPO advantages among test-passing rollouts.
scope_reason: Outcome includes implementation quality (precision, minimality, side effects, consistency) of LLM-generated repository patches.
gain_metric: Mean rubric-weighted quality score (1-5, LLM judge) on 30 DeepSWE tasks
baseline_name: Binary-outcome reward RL (same settings, no quality grading)
gain_quote:
Gagar achieves a mean quality score of 4.03
versus 3.70 for the baseline
gain_note: Figure 3 / Section 4.3, final shared checkpoint (step 28); judged by Claude Opus 5 on a fixed random sample of 30 DeepSWE tasks. Average win rate 69.8% among passing candidates; T1 share 25.4% to 34.3%. DeepSWE pass rate 62.2% vs 50.2% at step 28.
core_idea: During code-agent RL, an SFT-trained agentic grader jointly inspects all rollouts of a task, ranks test-passing ones on five quality criteria, and a sum-preserving rescaling shifts positive advantage toward higher-quality passes.
core_idea_checked: Gagar: dynamic-sampled mixed-outcome groups; grader (pre-RL SFT MiMo-V2.6-Pro) inspects trajectories, patches, repo and tests, assigns tiers and ranks, maps to discount factors; positive advantages are downweighted then rescaled to restore their original sum, failed advantages unchanged.
note: Training-time method for repository-level code agents; applicable to any test-verified coding RL, but evaluated only on proprietary MiMo models with an LLM-judge quality score and no code release.

title: From C to Idiomatic Rust: A Ship-of-Theseus Agentic Translation
technique_name: Ship-of-Theseus agentic C-to-Rust migration: c2rust lossless baseline, leaf-first call-graph ordering, per-function LLM reimplementation, two hard gates (Gate A compilation plus idiomaticity criteria, Gate B runtime behavioural equivalence with trace-divergence feedback), split into Phase 1 (signatures and bodies) and Phase 2 (global mutable state)
metrics: security (memory safety): SAFE% = 100(1 - (EX+NM)/(EX0+NM0)) where EX counts unsafe extern "C" fn declarations and NM counts #[no_mangle] annotations; RUST% = 100(1 - (PA+DU)/(PA0+DU0)) where PA counts raw pointer arithmetic sites and DU counts deep unsafe operations such as copy_nonoverlapping and write_bytes; also absolute counts of static mut globals wrapped and of unsafe blocks [all tool-static source counting]. readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): the five criteria C1 zero unsafe in function signatures, C2 slice-based buffer access, C3 no static mut, C4 no extern "C" on internal functions, C5 no C string or memory functions, enforced as hard errors at Gate A [tool-static]; SLOC of the resulting codebase. Correctness: compilation plus end-to-end behavioural equivalence (same output and state modification for the same input), checked after every port [execution]
benchmarks: Single case study, no benchmark suite: iodine, a production-quality DNS tunnel of approximately 12.5 kSLOC of C across 17 source files, with 168 functions ported and 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server). c2rust baseline counts: 178 EX, 73 NM, 319 PA, 144 DU
models: Not properly reported. The paper states translation was performed 'using subscription-based plans and the OpenCode-based infrastructure' and that 'the best result (fewest iterations) was achieved with Qwen3.6-27B'; no other model is named, no sizes or open/closed status for the others, and no per-model results are given. ChatGPT and Copilot are acknowledged only for proofreading the manuscript
baselines: The c2rust transpiler output (mechanically translated, non-idiomatic Rust) serves as the baseline against which SAFE% and RUST% are defined. No comparison against direct LLM C-to-Rust translation (the approach the paper argues against) and no comparison against other migration tools
effect_target_headline: Server porting (commits 1-31) lifts SAFE% to 72% and RUST% to 47%; client porting (commits 32-41) completes all 168 signatures at SAFE%=95%; static-mut elimination (commits 39-45, extending to the end of history) wraps the 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server) in atomics or mutexes, lifting RUST% to its final 57%. The final codebase is approximately 10.3 kSLOC of idiomatic Rust across 16 files, translated from an original 12.5 kSLOC C codebase, with no unsafe extern "C" function declarations and no static mut left in the evaluated code. Client porting and static-mut elimination cut the client's unsafe blocks from roughly 86 to 40. Residual gap: five signal-handler EX type aliases and six #[no_mangle] entry-point annotations, and 99 PA and 99 DU uses confined to FFI boundary adapters
effect_correctness_headline: Functional equivalence was verified end-to-end: after each of the 168 function ports and each of the 37 static mut wrappings (16 client, 21 server), Gate B ran the tunnel against the public resolver under real traffic for 30 s or more, verified curl download and netperf through the tunnel, and passed a wire-format integration test
notes: ELIGIBILITY NOTE: this is a translation/migration paper, so a reviewer could route it to the 'adjacent' side list (LLM refactoring of human-written code, EC4). It was included because the evaluated artifact is new Rust code that the LLM wrote (from a C source and a transpiled baseline), the five idiomaticity criteria and the safety counts are explicitly non-functional properties of that generated code, and the technique is an intervention (an agentic compile-plus-runtime feedback loop) designed to improve them. Other caveats. (1) The models are essentially unreported: only Qwen3.6-27B is named, as the one needing fewest iterations, and the claim that 'a particular model choice does not materially affect the outcome' is asserted without any supporting data. The agent tooling 'rtk' and 'OAC' is named but never explained or cited. (2) Single case study on one 12.5 kSLOC program; no repeated runs, no variance, no statistical test, and no comparison against the direct-LLM-translation baseline the paper argues against. (3) SAFE% and RUST% are author-defined composite metrics; they deliberately omit the raw unsafe count (justified as not penalising correct refactoring), and the headline 'no unsafe extern "C" function declarations' sits slightly in tension with SAFE% = 95% (the residual is five signal-handler EX type aliases plus six #[no_mangle] annotations). (4) Correctness is verified thoroughly but qualitatively; no pass rate or test-count figure is given, and the runtime oracle depends on a live public DNS resolver, which is not a reproducible test environment. (5) Notable negative finding worth recording: batching three Mutex wrappings produced a live deadlock that compiled and passed static checks but stalled transfers at zero bytes, and POSIX getopt() externs (optarg, optind, opterr, optopt) were found to be unwrappable and were deferred. (6) The process is explicitly human-in-the-loop: type deduplication, FFI adapter scaffolding and lock-wrapping orchestration were handled by a human as exceptions, so the 37 developer-hours figure mixes agent and human effort. (7) No artifact release; the only URL is upstream iodine (https://code.kryo.se/iodine/). (8) No contamination discussion, despite iodine being a long-standing public open-source project. (9) Figures 1, 2 and 3 extracted poorly (the three-column code listing in Figure 1 and the metric plot in Figure 3 are interleaved), but all quoted numbers come from the running text of Section 4.3 and the Validation paragraph.
family_reason: Per-function LLM rewrites are driven by compile gates (idiomaticity as hard errors) and runtime trace-divergence feedback.
scope_reason: Outcome is memory safety/idiomaticity of LLM-rewritten Rust in a C-to-Rust migration of an existing project, i.e. LLM editing of human-written code rather than generation from a specification.
gain_metric: SAFE% (share of c2rust extern C fn and no_mangle artefacts removed)
gain_quote: porting (commits 32–41) completes all 168 signatures at SAFE%=95%;
gain_note: Baseline value 0 follows from the definition (SAFE% is measured relative to the c2rust baseline counts 178 EX, 73 NM); RUST% reaches 57%. Single case study (iodine, 12.5 kSLOC), human orchestration, model mostly unreported (best with Qwen3.6-27B); no comparison with direct LLM translation.
core_idea: Start from a lossless c2rust translation and replace functions leaf-first with LLM reimplementations that must pass a compile gate enforcing five idiomatic-Rust criteria and a runtime equivalence gate with trace-divergence feedback.
core_idea_checked: c2rust baseline, call-graph leaf-first ordering, agentic per-function reimplementation, Gate A (compilation plus idiomaticity criteria C1-C5) and Gate B (runtime behavioural equivalence with trace diff), Phase 1 signatures and bodies then Phase 2 static mut wrapping.
note: Workshop case study of migrating one C project to Rust; tied to language migration of an existing codebase.

title: QiMeng-Kernel: Macro-Thinking Micro-Coding Paradigm for LLM-Based High-Performance GPU Kernel Generation
